Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. I hold in my hand the St. John Telegraph-Journal for March 19, 1932, which contains the report of a speech delivered in the New Brunswick legislature on Friday last by the Minister of Public Works for that province, in which reference is made to myself. The report states:
In Gloucester the ex-Postmaster General had made charges which, if based on facts, would have been grave.
At his request, Hon. Mr. Stewart continued, an official from the federal government had investigated the charges, which were disproven.
The complaints I made to the department were not reported on at all. A report was submitted by Mr. Carter, referring to only one complaint which, after all, was not made to him by myself, and in that connection he stated that no federal money had been expended on that particular road. When I was 'speaking on February 23 the Minister of Labour interrupted to state that on none of the roads mentioned by me in connection with my complaints had federal money been expended. I differed with the minister and repeated the statement that federal grants had been made in connection with the roads upon which my complaints were based. I have before me a report submitted by the Minister of Public Works of the province of New Brunswick, which was laid on the table of the legislature last week and which gives the list of works for which federal aid has been received. The name of every road mentioned by me on February 23 is to be found in that list.
I take objection to the statement that the complaints or charges which I had to make have been disproved. That is not the case, and I am prepared to stand by what I stated at that time.

That, in the opinion of this house, it is desirable that the Dominion government should cooperate to a greater extent with the provincial government in order to assist the maritime fisheries in the province of Quebec.
He said: I am bringing this motion to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, because a similar motion was adopted by the legislature of Quebec at the instance of the hon. member who represents the county of Charlevoix-Saguenay, Mr. Rochette, in the local house, seconded by his colleague for Gaspe, Mr. Chouinard.
It is not my intention to relate the history of the fishing industry in the province of Quebec. Suffice it to say that the history of the new world and of Quebec is intimately connected with the fisheries of the Atlantic seaboard, part of which is in the province
of Quebec. Who does not remember reading in the history of Canada that in the early days of its settlement our fishermen from Brittany and the Basque country used to come and fish in the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence, in the river itself?
In the early days of New France, and after the conquest, our fisheries were subjected to all sorts of troubles. Even after confederation several cases were taken as far as the privy council to determine the respective jurisdictions of the federal and provincial governments. The last judgment rendered in 1920 declared the administration and control of the fisheries of the interior to be in the provincial government, but that jurisdiction over the fisheries in salt water rested with the federal authorities, subject to the qualification that the provincial jurisdiction was supreme in so far as the soil of the province was concerned. Paragraph number two of the order in council dated February 13, 1922, which gave the administration of the fisheries to the province of Quebec, reads:
That as under the privy council decision of November 30, 1920, the province has the exclusive power to grant the right to fix engines to the soil, where the soil is vested in the crown in the right of the province, so far as such engines and the affixing of them do not interfere with the right of the public to fish or prevent the regulation of the right of fishing by private persons without the aid of such engines.
After this judgment of the privy council had been rendered, several orders in council were passed by both the federal and provincial governments vesting in the province of Quebec the administration of the fisheries in salt waters within the limits of the province. Since the provincial government has had control of the administration of the fisheries within the limits of the province they have made marvellous progress. A department called the Service des Pecheries Maritimes, with Mr. Gibault, an expert in fisheries, at its head, was created, which department is now presided over by the Hon. Mr. Laferte. Since that time an amount has been included in the annual estimates of his department to help the development of the fishing industry. The present government has rendered more assistance to this industry than any previous government. I think I am safe in saying that approximately $300,000 is spent annually to develop the fisheries within the limits of the province.
The provincial government has given assistance to the fishermen by the distribution of guns and ammunition with which to destroy the porpoises, which have caused great trouble to the fishermen during the last few years. A grant of $4 per keel foot is given towards the
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

construction of new schooners, and also a subsidy of twenty-five per cent of the total cost of equipping such vessels, up to the sum of $500. These subsidies have been of great assistance to the fishermen in remodelling their fishing apparatus and tackle, as well as providing work during the slack seasons. Apart from this, the provincial government has carried on public works and undertakings on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, in the county which I represent, to provide assistance for destitute fishermen. This has been especially the case during the past few years, during which time poor fishing conditions have prevailed on the north shore. It has been said that the porpoises are the great cause of trouble and annoyance to the fishermen and might be considered as one of the reasons for the poor conditions which have prevailed on the north shore, but I do not think that is the case. The problem which faces the fishermen is that of selling their fish on the domestic and foreign markets. Previously, fish could be dried or salted, but to-day the public require fresh fish, and this product controls the market. The fisheries of the province will meet with success and come into their own only when their efforts are directed towards the production of fresh fish.
At the present time there are between four and five thousand vessels engaged in fishing and employing between ten and twelve thousand people. In 1930 the value of the production was $2,502,998, the salt water production being valued at $1,976,798 and the production from interior waters, $526,200. This question is of vital importance to the county of Charlevoix-Saguenay, which I have the honour to represent, because a large portion of the people living on the north shore of the river derive their livelihood from the fisheries. This is true also of a large part of the population of the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure. Deep water fishing is to be. found along the north shore and I remember a few years ago when buyers from Nova Scotia, such as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysboro (Mr. Duff), the former member for Lunenburg, and some of his friends used to purchase fish from our people.

We do yet.
Mr. CASGRAIN. They do yet.
No industry, however great it may be, can expand unless its affairs receive wise administration and a methodical program of expansion is carried on. The last year the federal government had the administration of the fisheries it spent in the province of Quebec about $88,000. At that time the maritime provinces received about one million dollars

and the province of British Columbia, approximately $400,000. To-day the maritime provinces and British Columbia receive equal assistance while the province of Quebec has not received any subsidy since the year 1922. The federal government derives its revenues from all the provinces and, to my mind, when distributing subsidies it should give to each province a share proportionate to its population and to the need for the development of the fishing industry.
If my information is correct, the federal government receives about twenty-five per cent of its revenue from provinces from the province of Quebec. The average budget of the Department of Fisheries amounts to about $2,000,000 and, based on revenue received, Quebec should receive about $500,000. In other words, the Dominion government should spend half a million dollars in the development of the fisheries in Quebec, As I said a moment ago, the maritime provinces receive about $1,000,000 a year, and it would appear that they are receiving our share. Our province is the natural outlet for the products of the fisheries of the east, and yet the share of assistance to which we are entitled goes to help the maritimes to shut out our fishermen from their own markets.
No doubt the objection will be raised that as Quebec has control over its own fisheries it should look after them. Quebec controls its fisheries in the same manner as it controls its agriculture, mines and natural resources, and the federal government makes a contribution by way of subsidies to the development of agriculture and mining within the province. The federal government maintains in Quebec sixty-four demonstration farms and has a remount depot at St. Joachim. The government cooperates with the provincial government in the raising of sheep and hogs, and cooperates in the providing of assistance along other lines. The federal government also conducts scientific research in bacteriology and mining and has financed expeditions under the control of the Department of the Interior. All this has been done although the province controls its own natural resources. The federal government is seeking markets outside of Canada for our wheat. Why should the same assistance not be given to the fishing industry in my province? Instead of helping the fishing industry, the federal government last year imposed a duty on goods coming from Italy, with the result that the Italian government through Mussolini has imposed a duty of 15 per cent on fish coming from Canada. This affects in particular dried cod for which Italy offered a profitable market to the fishermen of Quebec.

.	Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
Instead of aiding the fishing industry which is one of the largest in Quebec, the government, by their tariff changes of last year, have injured it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: How?

On account of the imposition by the federal government of those duties that were placed against Italy, the Italian government imposed a duty of 15 per cent against dried cod for which, prior to that time, the fishermen of Quebec had a good market in Italy and also in Germany.
I have not Germany particularly in mind now.
I know the outlet for cod was more especially in Italy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There are other countries in the same position.

That may be so, but this action on the part of the federal government has been detrimental to my province and particularly to the marketing of our cod.
There is in Ottawa a biological service with stations at St. Andrews and Halifax, but we have nothing of that kind in Quebec. This branch of the Department of Fisheries conducts scientific research work and has technical men carrying on investigations and practical tests. I am informed that thirty-five investigations were made in the maritime provinces through this branch of the fisheries service in Ottawa and am advised that no similar research work has been carried on in Quebec. Investigations of this character might have been carried on along the north shore of the St. Lawrence in regard to halibut, scallops and lobsters, which I am told also abound in that district. Last July, due to the efforts of Mr. Copley Amory, a resident of the United States, a gentleman who has large interests on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, a scientific convention was held at a place below the seven islands, where this gentleman has an extensive establishment. Gentlemen were invited there from all parts of the world including Denmark and Norway, and I understand representatives from the provincial government also attended.
I am told the Deputy Minister of Fisheries was invited to be present, but I do not know whether the federal government gave any assistance in connection with this convention in order to help the people who are really making an effort to discover a solution of our problems and to develop the fisheries. I have not before me the report of the work of that convention.

There is also in operation under control of the Department of Fisheries, for the benefit of the maritimes and British Columbia, a fishery intelligence service furnishing information to fishermen as to water temperatures and movements of fish, but in Quebec we have not had the benefit of such a service. There is also in operation under the control of the Department of Fisheries, for the benefit of the maritime provinces, a fish collection service, a service which has often placed the purchaser in contact with the fisherman. We have never had in Quebec the benefit of such a service. The best service which fishermen of Quebec have had in order to help them to market their fish was through the efforts of the provincial government in assisting in the establishment of a special department through La Societe Cooperative Federe which has aided farmers and fishermen in marketing their products.
In the past, fish, salted, dried and pickled was accepted in the markets of the world; to-day things have changed and there is a much greater demand for fresh fish, the sale of which is more remunerative. Our fishermen of the north shore of the St. Lawrence, are however, not able to adopt these new methods in order to compete with other people on the markets of the world for fresh fish, because they have no money to build, equip and maintain the modern refrigerating plants necessary to preserve their fish and bait. Being far away from the large centres and being served only once a week in summer by a steamboat service, the fishermen of the north shore are thus at a disadvantage with other fishermen. In the province of Quebec, 90 per cent of the fresh fish used is imported for the most part from the states of New England and from British Columbia. On account of the lack of refrigerating plants our fishermen are compelled to sell at a low price to the export trade 60 per cent of their production, the greater part of which is salted, dried, or pickled fish. The only thing the federal government is doing is to supply the fishermen with plans and designs for the refrigerating plants; no subsidy or help of any kind has ever been given in that connection. The provincial government is considering the adoption of a system for establishing along the north shore of the St. Lawrence and other places where there are many fishermen, some of these refrigerating plants, but of course the cost of this would be very high and as they would not be able to obtain the help of the fishermen who are very poor, they require the assistance of the federal government.
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

Let me now quote a few paragraphs from the publication known as Les Ressources Na-turelles de Quebec, 1924:
'Translation):
The gulf of St. Lawrence is still in its infancy as regards the development of its fisheries. There are vast stretches of coast and numerous "banks" which have never been fished, except by the antiquated hook-and-line methods. Yet these waters are one of the world's chief congregating places for the cod, while many other varieties, including halibut and the unrivalled Atlantic salmon, are also more or less numerous in certain localities, and sea trout swarm in the brackish waters of the rivers where they meet the tide water.
Strange to say, most of the fish consumed in the province has been coming from the United States. Advertisements of fresh cod shipped direct from Portland, Maine, frequently appear in the Montreal papers. More remarkable still, fish from the Pacific coast is advertised and sold as far east as Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal, 3,000 miles or more from the waters where they are caught, while the salmon and cod and other fine varieties of fish at the very door of the province have been exported in a salted or dried condition to Europe, the West Indies and the United States. It would appear, therefore, that opportunity exists for enterprising fishermen to build up a considerable home market for their catch.
Our sea fisheries like many other industries are at the present time suffering through lack of proper markets. It is most essential that something be done to help them, because in aiding them we help the country at large and are building up a real Canadian industry which at all times in our history has been considered basic. Lest the government say that they are powerless as regards the sea fisheries of Quebec, on account of the fact that the administration of the fisheries was taken over by the provincial government, let me read from the order in council passed in 1922 when the federal government transferred the administration of the fisheries to the provincial government:

The Minister recommends that the whole administration of the Department of Fisheries which is amen-ab!e to the Fisheries Act and regulations thereof should be transferred to the provincial authorities.
There is nothing in that order in council which prevents the federal government giving assistance to the provincial authorities. The administration of all the laws of the federal parliament formerly administered through the Department of Fisheries, is transferred to the provincial government of Quebec. As I said before, our agriculture and our mines are helped by the federal government, but we have not been able to obtain any assistance from this government for the fisheries in Quebec. The reason I have placed this resolution

on the order paper is that there seems to be growing at the present time in Quebec a greater interest in what should be done in the way of developing the fishing industry. I have in my hand a pamphlet which is called Le Canada Frangais de Quebec, February, 1932, and under the heading of Le Developpement des Pecheries de la Province de Quebec, Professor Louis Berube has given many points which will be of interest to the house.
But as my time is rapidly passing I shall content myself with bringing this article to the attention of the government. The article entitled Le Developpement des pecheries de la province de Quebec, is divided under four headings as follows: Stabilisation de 1'industrie de la peche; Stabilisation et amelioration des conditions de vie chez les pficheurs; L'apport de la science au developpement des pecheries; L'apport de l'Etat au developpement des pecheries, and under the last heading this gentleman states:
(Translation):
"The carrying out of an exhaustive program of our maritime fishery development requires the cooperation of all and especially that of the government at Ottawa. Indeed, there are, as we shall later on discover, questions which are directly relevant of the jurisdiction and activities of the Dominion government and without the solution of which the activities of the provincial government are, so to speak, paralysed. There are, moreover, problems in which the cooperation of the two can but double the results to be obtained.
First, we shall insure the freedom of the seas, the protection of markets and the grading of products; in the second, scientific research and financial aid."
Further on he says:
The protection to be given to markets is very intimately linked with the tariff problem. The Dominion government, which, is solely in control, can therefore, alone, give the necessary protection' to our local markets, by levying a duty on foreign products; again alone it can foster our export markets by special tariff treaties. We might mention, as an instance, the 15 per cent duty levied at present by Italy on our dry fish. The Dominion government by agreeing to a tariff reduction on other articles would perhaps succeed in overcoming this drawback.
Other articles and other suggestions have been brought to my attention since this resolution has been on the order paper. One is in the form of a memorandum which I have received from Mr. S. J. Flynn, secretary-treasurer of the county of Gaspe. In paragraph one of the memorandum, under the heading, Aide du Gouvemement federal, appears this suggestion:
(Translation):
Finally, the Dominion government should further assist our fishermen by improving our fishing harbours, building breakwater barriers,

Maritim.e Fisheries, Quebec
dredging, etc., by establishing in all parts of the country meteorological stations to signal the approach of disastrous storms, help our fish markets by resorting to a protective tariff and the activities of its officials abroad or otherwise.
Further on he says:
We believe that a loyal agreement between the Dominion and provincial governments would place at our disposal a minimum of $300,000 per year, that is 50 per cent at least of the theoretical amount due and which could be used as follows:
1.	Establish a fishing centre:- _
(a)	Oceanographic station-Biological.
Oceanographic station-Economical.
This Dominion station would be the only means at our disposal to establish a permanent link with the International Council for sea exploration, and of which Canada forms part as well as France and the United States (American section).
(b)	Refrigerator for bait (Dominion Act, grant of 75 per cent).
(c)	Freezing plant (Dominion Act, grant of 30 per cent).
(d)	Service of fish collecting (Dominion service which is already in use in the other provinces) .	_
2.	Organize a more effective service of inspection (Dominion Act), This is requested by almost (95 per cent) the entire fishing industry of Canada;
3.	Organize an effective supervision and protective service: observance of the treaties and laws. Assistance to navigation, protection of the various coasts of the province of Quebec, Labrador, Anticosti, Madeleine Islands, etc., etc.; which is done, at present, through Halifax. Our own protective service was abolished in 1922.
4.	Organize a service of commercial and industrial intelligence for fishermen, fish dealers and heads of industries. (A service recommended since 1893 by F. X. Joncas). All the provinces, with the exception of Quebec, possess such a service.
5.	Begin a reasonable improvement of the ports which carry on fishing on a small scale;
6.	Organize a scientific, technical and administrative staff.
These gentlemen, as will be observed, are apparently very much concerned about the development of the fishing industry in the province of Quebec; they say that the best development of that industry cannot be obtained for the reasons mentioned unless the federal government give further assistance and cooperation to the provincial government. Since a similar debate took place last session in the local assembly at Quebec many delegations have interviewed the provincial govem-, ment. There was a delegation on the 15th of March, 1932, from Gaspe which was received by Hon. Mr. Hector Laferte, Minister of Fisheries in the province of Quebec, and on the 17th of March a delegation from Gaspe made representations to the chamber of commerce.
41761-82i
March 15, 1932. "Delegation from the Gaspe Peninsula to the Legislature. The hon. Mr. Hector Laferte, Minister of Colonization, Fish and Game receives an important delegation from the Gaspe Peninsula and the North
March 17, 1932. "The fishermen of the Gaspd Peninsula, and the fish dealers of Quebec wish to establish reciprocal markets. The former met the Chamber of Commerce. Both groups discussed the means to take so as to establish a Quebec market for the Gaspe products and vice versa."
Another reason which has prompted me to bring this resolution before the house is that I noticed in the newspapers a few months ago that other provinces which seem to have been well looked after by the government at all times have been seeking further assistance from this government. In the Montreal Star of January 27, 1932 I read this:
Fishermen Urge Government Aid Officers of Maritime Body interview Hon. E. N.
Rhodes
Ottawa, Jan. 27-(C.P.)-Claiming that nothing has been done for the fishermen comparable to what the Dominion government has done for agriculture, and asking for a comprehensive and intensive effort to place the Canadian fishing industry on a profitable and business-like basis, delegates from the United Maritime Fishermen presented an appeal yesterday to Hon. E. N. Rhodes, Minister of Fisheries.
Alfred Hanlon, Canso, N.S., president, and Bruce Burke, Drum Head, N.S., vice-president, laid before the Minister a resolution drawn up at a meeting of the federation in Halifax last Friday. Mr. Rhodes gave the brief considerable study, but advised the delegation that the department was doing everything possible under present economic conditions, to grapple with the unsatisfactory situation existing in this important industry. He will discuss the matter with the maritime officials again to-day, but no definite decision as to what extent the government will be able to act, will be available for some time.	,
The United Maritime Fishermen asked the government to place research men in the field to study marketing agents in foreign countries to represent the organized fishermen, broadcast regularly the trend of prices and market conditions, and to carry on with a competent staff of field men, educational work in production and selling.
So in case the government does anything for the people of these other provinces I should like the same consideration to be extended at the same time to the people that I have the honour to represent in this house as well as to the fishermen of Bonaventure and Gaspe counties and of the province of Quebec in general.
Another article which struck me was headed, "Fishing Industry facing Big Crisis-Maritime M. P. suggests solution in Canadian Club
address." The article goes on to quote my
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

genial friend from Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst), who is keenly interested in the development of the fishing industry in the maritime provinces.
And in Quebec too.

And in Quebec too. We are on the same ground there. My hon. friend is quoted in this despatch as follows:
Another remedy for the fishing industry was to be found in trade treaties, and the member for the Queens-Lunenburg constituency of Nova Scotia added that other remedies had been suggested to the government which he did not feel at liberty to discuss but he did believe that with encouragement the industry was going to come through.
If other remedies have been suggested to the government which my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg did not feel at liberty to discuss, when those remedies are brought forward I wish to see them applied for the benefit of the people of the other provinces and the country at large. The people of the province I represent should be given the same benefit and advantage as the people of other provinces. My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg went on to say:
The speaker realized, because of the geographical conditions of the Dominion, that there were difficulties in the way of developing the fresh fish industry. Prime cod was being sold at a cent and a half a pound at the wharf and the fisherman could not understand the reason for the spread between the wholesale and retail prices. The fresh fish industry had been hard hit by the United States tariffs, which had practically shut out its chief market, and the extension of the Canadian market for such a perishable product presented many difficulties. Experiments were being tried with chemical ice which when it dissolved left no trace and no water, and other methods were also being tried to increase the per capita consumption in Canada, which would increase the livelihood of the men.
All these are reasons, Mr. Speaker, which have led me to believe that I would be derelict in my duty as a member of this house if I did not bring these facts to the attention of parliament and the government. In order to remedy the present existing conditions in the province of Quebec I think there should be a conference between the Dominion government and the provincial government at which the foundation of an entente could be laid defining the scope or field of operation of the province and of the dominion in order that out of such a conference proper cooperation between the two governments might be obtained. It is with this intention, sir, that I have brought this resolution before the house and that I submit it humbly for the consideration of the government. I do not want to play any politics in this matter. In presenting fMr. Casgrain.]
this resolution I am not seeking for myself or the party to which I belong any political advantage or benefit, and I trust that that will be the attitude of all hon. gentlemen on this question relating to an industry which is one of the largest and oldest in the province of Quebec and in the eastern part of Canada, and which, like other industries, has been suffering from lack of markets and possibly from lack of subsidies which may be necessary to develop it in the way it should be developed. True, the provincial government is doing its best to develop that industry, but it has not been able, within the last few years of its administration of fisheries, to develop scientific and technical men, and also to carry on various establishments such as those maintained here in Ottawa in the federal Department of Fisheries, which have been in existence for a good many years, and are about the best on the continent of America.
I think Mr. Speaker, that the resolution should carry because I am not asking anything unreasonable. My request is for further assistance and cooperation from this government. We have been asked to develop certain programs whereby we might help the government through its present financial difficulties. Here is a practical suggestion in which cooperation should not be lacking, should not be refused and should be forthcoming from this government and from my genial friend the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) who was at one time Minister of Fisheries, and who is thoroughly familiar with the matter now before us.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the ordinary course of events this resolution would have been spoken to by the Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) who, I regret to say, is not present this afternoon. Consequently in his absence I feel it incumbent upon me to say a few words in reply. I should have preferred to have had the opportunity of referring to data and materials which I would have had before me, had I known I would be called upon to say a word or two in this connection.
I do not think I can take any marked exception to the resolution, nor to the tenor of the remarks of the hon. member who sponsors it. I wish however in the course of my remarks to take exception to one or two of the statements he has made. The * resolution now before us reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is desirable that the Dominion government should cooperate to a greater extent with the provincial government in order to assist the maritime fisheries in the province of Quebec.

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
I should have preferred the wording of the resolution to be that the government should cooperate to the ''greatest possible extent,'[DOT] because the wording as it now appears in the resolution might indicate that there had been some lack of cooperation by the federal government in its association with the province of Quebec. In case anyone should be inclined so to interpret this resolution I wish to say at once that such an interpretation cannot properly be held. Especially is my statement true when we bear in mind that at one time the fisheries of the province of Quebec were under the full direction and control of the Department of Fisheries at Ottawa.
And they should have stayed there, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) says they should have remained there.
I think so, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I concur entirely with my hon. friends opposite in that point of view, and I do not for one moment wish to be understood as finding any fault, much less of attempting to impart any political flavour to this discussion when I say that the reason they are not still under the control of the federal government is that in the judgment of the then Minister of Fisheries, the present hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), Quebec had taken itself out of the control of the federal Department of Fisheries and set up its own house in the matter of fisheries control. My hon. friend who is sponsoring this resolution is familiar with that fact. So when he says that no industry can expand unless wise administration is given to it, in so far as that expression of opinion on his part is applicable to the lack of improvement in the fisheries of the province of Quebec, I must say the responsibility rests entirely with the Department of Fisheries in that province.
Coming back to the terms of the resolution, or that phase of it which would indicate, at least by inference, that there had not been complete cooperation with the dominion Department of Fisheries, let me say to my hon. friend that in my experience in the federal department I know of no instance where there was not complete and, I may say, harmonious and pleasant cooperation with the Department of Fisheries of the province of Quebec. I know of no instance where they sought our assistance and we did not respond. As a matter of fact, my mind goes back to one or two particular instances last year which
would bear out my statement. At that time there came up for consideration with respect to salmon fisheries common to Quebec and the province of New Brunswick, not only the question of season, but the method and the use of the implements incidental to fishing. That is to say, there were considered the size of nets to be used, the manner in which they were to be placed in the water, the length of leaders and all such things. In the city of Ottawa there was held a conference representative of all phases of the fisheries industry. One of the first things we did was to communicate with our friends in the Department of Fisheries of the province of Quebec and ask them to send a representative to the conference. With that request they complied, and we were favoured throughout the whole of the meetings with the presence of Mr. Gibault, representing the Department of Fisheries of the province of Quebec. Decisions arrived at at that time were unanimous, and made possible by complete cooperation between the Department of Fisheries in the province of Quebec and the federal department here in Ottawa.
My hon. friend has referred to that very unique conference held at Matameck on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, which was made possible by a gentleman to whom I think a word of praise might at this time properly be given. He is a distinguished citizen of the United States and has a summer residence near Matameck. Having lived there a number of years during the summer seasons he became very much attached to that area and its people. It was his desire to assist, amongst other things, the fishing industry as well as the. poor people in the vicinity, and arising from that desire he arranged the conference which lasted a week or ten days, and which cost him a large sum of money because he provided transportation and all facilities to the representatives present. He put his services, time and money to the use of the people of Canada, solely with the idea of assisting the people of the province of Quebec.
One of his first acts was to communicate with the department at Ottawa, asking that the department be represented. His communication arrived at a time when the house was in session and for that reason the Deputy Minister of Fisheries could not attend.. Arrangements were made, however, for the attendance of Doctor Huntsman, head of the biological board. During the whole of the conference he attended and represented the federal Department of Fisheries. There was also present Doctor Camsell, deputy minister of the federal Department of Mines.

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
I have mentioned these facts in passing to indicate to the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) that there has been complete cooperation between the federal and provincial departments. My hon. friend has referred to certain subsidies which he says have been given to the people of the maritime provinces and the people of British Columbia in which the province of Quebec has not participated. I know of none. The only direct subsidy in the fishing industry is the sum of $160,000 voted year after year which arises, as my hon. friend knows, out of the Halifax award.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It does not come out of
the funds of the treasury of Canada-
It is taken out of the consolidated fund. There is no reference in the act at all to the Halifax award.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend may differ
from me, but I adhere to my statement as originally given, with all due deference to my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill).

The United States paid
$4,500,000 to Canada and $1,000,000 to Newfoundland for certain privileges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, and it is the yield
upon that sum, at a fair interest rate, that has been divided among the fishermen.
Were there any subsidies for the construction of refrigeration plants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows,
I am speaking now without reference to the statute and with no notes before me, but I think he will find upon inquiry that the provisions of that act are applicable to the fishing industry throughout Canada. With reference to the cold storage act, if the fishermen of the province of Quebec wish to avail themselves of the provisions of that statute, it is just as open to them to do so as it is open to the fishermen of any other part of Canada.
My hon. friend has stated that the administration of the fisheries by the dominion costs something like $2,000,000 a year. As a matter of fact, there have been some reductions in the estimates of the Department of Fisheries. Speaking from memory, I think the reduction last year was about $345,000, and this year there has been another reduction of about $80,000, so the total expenditure is really less than $2,000,000. But my hon. friend would leave the impression that all this money was spent in other parts of Canada and not 
in Quebec. In the first place let me say that even if this were so Quebec has only itself to blame. They cannot come here now and take the position that, having eaten their cake, they still want it. They deliberately took themselves out from under the direction and control of the Dominion Department of Fisheries, but in any case it is not so that this entire amount is spent in portions of Canada other than Quebec. It is quite competent for the Quebec Department of Fisheries, for the fishing industry of that province or for individual fishermen there to avail themselves of the services of the federal department. In my own experience I have known many occasions when that has been done.
My hon. friend has referred to the fact that there is a biological station at St. Andrews and another on the Pacific coast, while there is none in the province of Quebec. It does not follow that the work of a biological station is confined to the locality in which the station is located; as a matter of fact, if proper work is done in the field of biology in connection with our fisheries, it can be done as well at St. Andrews as it could be done at any other place on the Atlantic seaboard. The point I wish to make, however, is that the statistics obtained, the results of experiments carried out and all the knowledge gleaned through the expenditure of that money and the work of the scientists, are made available to the people of the province of Quebec just as they are made available to the people of the other provinces. The same thing is true in connection with the engineering branch of the Department of Fisheries. Plans and specifications with respect to the construction of cold storage plants, ships and all the rest of it, together with all the data that has been obtained, are available to the fishermen of all parts of the country, without regard to provinces.
My hon. friend has stated that the federal department provided a fish collection service in the maritime provinces while it did not provide that service in Quebec. I could very well say that Quebec is running its own fisheries and that this matter should be attended to by the government of that province, but I wish to point out to my hon. friend that there was a limited extension of this service to cover a portion of the Nova Scotia coast which did not possess the facilities found in practically all other coast waters of the maritime provinces, Quebec and British Columbia. These facilities consist in the main of local steamship services, and if my hon. friend would take the trouble to look at the

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
estimates he would find that each year we vote hundreds of thousands of dollars for subsidies and subventions to steamships and packets both on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts in order to provide these services, and the provision of these services has brought about improved transportation facilities so far as the fisheries in Quebec are concerned.
Arising out of the interruption of my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff)-to which I do not take exception-if I might say so with all deference, without wishing to find any fault and without canvassing the ground that has been covered already, I would suggest that his attention might be far better directed towards the return to federal control of the fisheries of the province of Quebec.

Especially now that we have
a minister from Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite so. I believe a unified direction of our fisheries is greatly to be desired. If we tried to direct our fisheries by provincial control, each province differing from the other in method, with resultant duplication of service, we would have a tremendously expensive and cumbersome machine, and we would get nowhere in the way of national direction.

I am afraid the
answer from Quebec will be "What we have we hold."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Quite so, but that is purely a matter for our friends in Quebec. My hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough has been very frank in his expression of opinion, and I wish to be equally frank and say that I entirely concur in what he has said. Let me repeat that I know of no case where we have refused to cooperate or to give every assistance within our power and our competence. Just here let me say this: During the time I had the honour of heading the Department of Fisheries it was a matter of great pleasure to me to have some contacts with the fisheries department of the province of Quebec. In every respect our relations were harmonious, cordial, and I hope mutually helpful. As a matter of fact, one of the last acts I performed while head of that department was to conclude an arrangement to provide fish demonstrations, the idea being to enlarge the market for fish by teaching the housewives better methods of preparing them. We employed the services of a lady who is known throughout the continent of North America as one of the foremost exponents of the art of fish cookery, and I
wrote the Minister of Fisheries of Quebec and said I should like him to cooperate with us in that movement. I received a very nice answer; he said he would be very happy to join with us, and to-day the province of Quebec is paying the salary of a lady who was associated with Mrs. Spencer, who is able to demonstrate to the people of that province in the French language. Naturally we started that campaign in Ottawa, but the very next place where the demonstrations were carried on was the city of Montreal. They are being given there to-day, as they have been for some weeks, and I believe this action has brought about good results so far as the industry and the province are concerned. I merely mention that as a concrete example of how we have endeavoured in every possible way to cooperate with the provincial government.
Bearing in mind what I have said, so far as I am concerned I have no objection to this resolution, though as I said in the first instance it might have asked that the government should cooperate to the greatest possible extent, instead of saying that we should cooperate to a greater extent.

I wish, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Cas-grain) on bringing this matter before the house. He has done so, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has said, in a very lucid manner and has furnished us with much valuable information. This dual control of our fisheries by the dominion and the province is a very, very old question. When I had the honour in 1897 to be the candidate of the Liberal party in the county of Gaspe, the then premier of the province scored heavily by announcing during the campaign the decision of the privy council to the effect that the fisheries were within the provincial jurisdiction, and that thereafter the province would control them. That practice continued until control reverted to the dominion. In 1922 Quebec again secured jurisdiction over the fisheries. No matter what the position is at the present time, it is not satisfactory. When I had the honour of being elected for the county of Bonaventure thirty years ago, all the coast was lined with fishermen's huts. We had important fisheries at Port Daniel, Gascons, Paspebiac, Bonaventure, and Caplan. The men of these districts earned their livelihood in the fishing industry. For some reason or other the industry has declined and to-day a very small number of men earn their living in that way.
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

In 1922, the provincial authorities relieved the dominion to a great extent by taking over control of the fisheries. Our fisheries are one of our great natural resources and anything that will develop them in Quebec will be for the benefit of Canada generally. Whatever may be the reason, it is an unfortunate fact that our fisheries in Chaleur bay are not being developed. We have provincial control in certain things and federal control in others. The Minister of Finance has referred to numerous lines of steamers subsidized for the benefit of the maritime provinces to assist in the development of these fisheries. So far as my constituents are concerned we used to have a line between Gaspe and Dalhousie, New Brunswick, but that line was discontinued years ago. The people in my constituency are complaining of the rates they have to pay on the Canadian National railways to gain access to the large markets of Quebec and Montreal. I am not prepared to discuss this phase of the ' question, having only this morning received a copy of the report of the interview that the representatives of the fishermen in the Gaspe district had with the provincial Minister of Fisheries, but from glancing through the long report I conclude that things are not as they should be. The Minister of Finance, who is probably the best-informed man in this house on the question of our fisheries, should make a point of seeing that something be done, because the condition of these fisheries is not what it should be.
I had an opportunity last week of introducing to the Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) a deputation from New Brunswick and Quebec with regard to salmonfishing in the Chaleur bay district. There is long-standing dissent between the anglers and the fishermen of our Gaspe salmon. The dominion regulations requiring the raising of nets from Sunday till Monday morning is a great obstacle to the net fishermen. While the Deputy Minister of Fisheries, who is an authority on these matters, contends that it is in the interests of the salmon fishermen themselves that they should get out into the centre of the river, they take objection on the ground that they lose the best runs of the season. Be that as it may, the department has again turned down the request made by the fishermen, and I think a meeting should be arranged as soon as possible between the dominion and the provincial authorities to see if some better understanding cannot be brought about.
The government of Quebec last week took steps towards the establishing of some freezing stations along the coast for the use of the [Mr. Marcil.l
fishermen. At the present time as the member for Charlevoix-Saguenay stated, the fishermen have to salt their fish, thus reducing its value by fifty per cent, and at the same time they find their markets in Brazil, the West Indies and elsewhere have shrunken to a very serious extent. In a word, our fishermen find themselves, in common with our other producers, in the unhappy position of a lack of markets. We have not the markets to-day to be prosperous as we had under the old regime of moderate tariffs. But whatever be the cause of the decline of our fisheries, both the dominion and the provinces are interested in their development and in finding new markets. In Quebec the provincial authorities have control of the fishing regulations at the present time, but when it comes to securing access to markets, cheap transportation and sale abroad we come into the federal domain. Means should be found of preserving the fish, giving cheap transportation, and securing access to foreign markets.
I hope this resolution will meet with the approval of the whole house. I have heard the question discussed many times, but the main trouble seems to be the conflict between provincial and federal control. I agree to some extent with the Minister of Finance that it is highly important that there should be uniform control of all our fisheries. In Montreal, where I have resided all my life, the fish that we eat during the winter comes largely from Maine and the maritime provinces. There is no reason why some understanding should not be arrived at by which our fishermen would be given a better market and increased remuneration for their work. Canada should be one of the first countries in the world as far as the fishing industry is concerned. We have some of the finest fish to be found anywhere. In order that we may get the fullest advantage from this great natural resource it is necessary that the difficulties between the province and the dominion should be arranged on a basis satisfactory to all concerned. I am glad the government has in charge of this department a man who is thoroughly conversant with the subject. The time has come when this question should be considered in earnest with a view to seeing whether we cannot do something to assist our fishermen who are in dire need.
A new factor must be considered in dealing with this question. American fishermen come to the waters of Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick for sport fishing, and some consideration must be given to these men. They spend a tremendous amount of

money in the pursuit of their sport, and I have -been told that it costs $200 for every salmon taken out of the Restigouche river. They observe the law to the fullest extent, they register every fish taken, and they give every assistance possible. The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mac-Laren) does me the honour of fishing every year -in my constituency. I trust he will be spared for many years to come to continue to enjoy this sport. He is a friend of the fishermen. Sir Douglas Hazen, a very prominent man in the maritime provinces, who was minister of marine and fisheries in the old days, is a frequent visitor to my constituency. On behalf of these men, I urge the dominion government not to turn a deaf ear to this question.
I can remember in the old days seeing the fishermen use dynamite and salt their catch in barrels, employing somewhat the same process as was used in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia with the oyster. The oyster has practically disappeared from Canada, except in Prince Edward Island. The time has come when assistance should be given to the fisherman. His life is a hard one, he leaves early in the morning not knowing when he will return. He has to face all sorts of weather and at times his income is small when compared with his labour. We have dual control over agriculture and mining, we should have similar control over our fisheries. I urge the government through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) and the Minister of Pensions and National Health to take up this question seriously and see if something cannot be done to improve the present condition of our fisheries.

Mr. Speaker, I rather welcome the opportunity which has been afforded by the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) for a general discussion of the fisheries, but before I proceed to discuss fisheries generally I want to say a word or two with reference to the hon. member's resolution. He confines his resolution to the province of Quebec, and from his closing remarks I gather that one of the motives for his doing this was that other districts were seeking relief and he did not want that relief granted until it was granted to the province of Quebec. I happened to be present with a delegation which waited upon the government with respect to the salt fish industry, with which the hon. member is most particularly concerned, and while they asked aid for their industry, they never at any time
asked aid only for the industry in Nova Scotia. They recognized frankly that any relief must be given equally to the four provinces which engage in this industry.
The hon. member stated that inasmuch as the province of Quebec pays some twenty-five per cent of the revenue of Canada, at least $500,000 should be paid to the province as aid in the development of its fisheries. The first answer to this was given by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) when he stated that the province of Quebec had chosen to administer its own fisheries since 1922, the authority for this being in an order in council which we can safely assume was passed at the solicitation of the province. I remind my hon. friend, but not in a partisan spirit, of the dictum laid down some few years ago by his own leader. The right hon. gentleman stated that he considered it to be a vicious principle that one taxing authority should raise revenue and give it to another taxing authority to spend without any control being held over such expenditures. I think that is a complete answer to any demand for a cash subsidy to be paid to the province of Quebec in aid of its fisheries.
I agree with the hon. member for Antigo-nish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) that it would be in the best interests of the fisheries of the dominion as a whole if the fisheries of the province of Quebec were placed under federal control as are those of the three eastern provinces. When the Minister of Finance made that suggestion the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) interjected the remark "What we have we hold." He might at least have completed the quotation by saying: "What we have not we're after."
Having given my reasons for not being able to support the resolution in the terms in which it appears, I want to say something about the problems which face the industry generally. The problems which face the Gaspe peninsula are the same as those confronting the fishermen along the whole coast of Nova Scotia, especially in my own constituency, which has the largest salt fishing fleet in the world. Before dealing with these problems, let me refer first to the causes thereof. The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and the hon. member for Char-levoix-Saguenay have suggested that in some measure tariffs are responsible for the present difficulties. If they mean by that the tariffs of the Dominion of Canada, then I cannot agree; if they mean the tariffs of other countries, I admit that to some extent that is true.

There are three primary reasons for the difficulties which now face the salt fishing industry of the world. First, there is a general world depression which must be faced when you have a product which must be sold in the export market. Second, and accentuating the first in a peculiar manner in so far as the fishing industry is concerned, there is the almost complete collapse of purchasing power in Brazil, one of the largest salt fish importing countries in the world. A similar collapse, perhaps not so great, has taken place in the purchasing power of Spain and Portugal. Third, there is the fact that nearly all the great salt fish producing countries in the world have increased their production. Take for instance, Norway, Iceland, Newfoundland and Great Britain; all of these countries are entering the markets of the world with increasing quantities of fish, and the result is that there are more fish than can be absorbed by the consumer. Practically the only markets left to us are those of the West Indies, Cuba and Porto Rico.
The fishermen in the Gaspe section of the coast have been shipping their product to Spain and Portugal and, to a smaller degree, to Italy, but these markets have been almost completely closed.
This fisherman produces a superior product and he has been accustomed to a superior price. To-day he has to take the same price as all the others are taking in the export markets of the world, a price that is far below the cost of production. Added to all the difficulties of the depression, come those of the exchange situation. As I said, practi-tically the only markets which are left are Cuba, Porto Rico and the West Indian islands, and when we do business with those countries, all the exchange comes through New York. The exchange rate in regard to both the Canadian dollar and the pound sterling has been most uncertain, it fluctuates from day to day, and I think I may safely mention that the lowering in value of the pound sterling due to the action of Britain in going off the gold standard, which placed the pound at a lower value than the Canadian dollar, has given to the English exporter an advantage of from 20 to 25 per cent. 1 realize the difficulties of the exchange situation and I am not expressing anything but a personal view, but I am by no means anxious to see the Canadian dollar get back to par too quickly.
Par with what?
With the United States dollar.
Then the Canadian fishermen will get less.

No. These are fluctuations which do not affect the Canadian dollar internally but do affect our ability to sell abroad. Some of these things will right themselves, and if we have any faith in the future we must feel that they are going to do so in the course of time. Broadly, we see the natural reaction in that some of the great exporting countries are curtailing the production this year, so that we look forward with some hope towards increased prices next year. For the present year, however, our difficulty is apparent and real.
Having said that about the condition of the industry in general, because the industry in Gaspe in connection with salt and pickled fish is similar to that in Lunenburg, I should like to say to the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay that when he suggests that the remedy for his fishermen is that they handle fresh fish, he is speaking only a partial truth in the economic sense. Again I am voicing only a personal opinion. It seems to me that one of the most tragic blunders we made in the administration of the fisheries of this country was to endeavour to turn the individual fishermen scattered along thousands of miles of coast line into dealers in fresh fish. This cannot be done. Fresh fish is an extremely perishable product. It has to be taken quickly to the cold storage or else it deteriorates, and when it deteriorates it is no longer fresh. In Nova Scotia, by a system of collection boats, we have endeavoured to turn the entire coastline into the fresh fish industry, but this has proved altogether uneconomic and unsound and I believe it will prove equally so in the Gaspe peninsula. In my opinion, the remedy does not lie there; it lies in teaching our fishermen improved methods of conserving and curing. I am not satisfied that the salt fish, as we know it to-day, represents the ultimate in the production of cured fish at home by the individual fisherman. I am convinced research will show that much more can be done and that a much better quality of fresh and cured fish can be placed on the market by the individual fisherman working from his own fish house, than is being done at the present time, even in the Gaspe peninsula, where they have, as I have said, a superior type of salt fish.
Having said that and having tried to make it clear that the problems of the Gaspe peninsula are those of Nova Scotia, of Lunenburg county, let me say that I concur in the statement of the hon. member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil) that the fisherman to-day i3 in a really pitiable condition. I am talking now of the salt fisherman. Some of the fresh

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
fish industries are operating almost to capacity, but in those the fisherman receives only a pittance for that which he brings to port. But I pass over the fresh fish industry, because the two cannot be confused; each offers a different field for investigation and a different line for development. Further, with reference to the fresh fish industry in eastern Canada-and I am making no reference to British Columbia because I do not know anything about the fishing industry there-we sell a very substantial proportion of our catch in the home market where we are not subjected to the fluctuations of the export price and world conditions. The salt fish industry is entirely different.
Let me come now to my own constituency of Lunenburg. Some few years ago we had 120 vessels which operated out of that port, and at that time they were propelled mainly by sail. They carried crews of from twenty to twenty-five men. The method of fishing was that the men went two by two over the sides in dories and fished writh lines or trawl lines, which are long lines baited at intervals. When they got their catch they took it back to the mother ship, where it was salted, and eventually when the season expired or the vessel became loaded, she would return to port. A hundred vessels at that time meant direct employment to between 2,000 and 3,000 men. In fact, it meant something more than that: it meant indirect employment to thousands more, because when the fish were brought back they had to be cured; that is, they were brought back green salted and had to be washed and dried in the sun. That gave work for a portion of the year to a large number of people scattered along the coastline of the county. Then there were the shipyards, because the vessels in which our people fished were built in our own shipyards, using our own lumber, timber and materials so far as they were available. We imported cordage and canvas and the ironwork was largely fashioned by local blacksmiths. I can think of six such shipyards in Lunenburg county alone and an average annual pay-roll for one of them would be about $50,000, with another $50,000 spent in the same year on materials. That is an average year. To-day every one of those shipyards, with one exception, and that one is not building a fishing vessel, is closed.
Furthermore, the fish were exported in casks which were made of hardwood staves from trees which were cut locally by local labour and made in local cooperages. Speaking from memory, I believe there are a large number of them scattered throughout my constituency. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough (Mr. Duff), who has just come in, is thoroughly familiar with this because he has been in the salt fish trade all his life. A fair
average payroll for one of these cooperages would be from $10,000 to $15,000 a year, with material taking a like amount. Those cooperages are in a large measure closed down. The men who pack the fish, who work on the wharves, the docks, have practically lost their livelihood, and the fleet which was once 100 strong was last year down to forty-two. This year, if conditions remain as they are and without some measure of governmental assistance, I do not believe ten Lunenburg vessels will go to the banks to catch salt fish.
The method of operation has changed. Sail is giving way by degrees to the Diesel engine, but 'basically our fishermen still catch their fish, salt them and bring them in. What is the outcome unless we obtain relief? It must be the destruction of that industry. I have heard it argued by many that the farmer is in a like position. He is, and he is not. A farm is not perishable. A farmer may lose it, it is true, by a process of foreclosure, but it still remains a farm capable of production as it always was. A vessel property is perishable. The average situation of the vessels of the Lunenburg fleet is this: they are operated largely under the provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act. Each vessel is divided into sixty-four shares, and under the act one man will act as manager, owner or agent for the rest. The crew and the owner work on a share basis or on a kind of partnership scheme or venture. Each year, when a vessel goes out, the managing owner advances the money or guarantees an advance by the bank to outfit it for the voyage that year at a cost of $4,000 or $5,000. In former days when commodity prices were higher, the amount would be greater. He trusts to the success of the venture in the sale of fish to recoup himself for his advance, but for the last two years he has not been able to recoup himself, and nearly every vessel fishing out of Lunenburg is in debt from three thousand dollars up to eight thousand dollars, and some for much more than that. That may not seem a staggering amount when you remember that the vessels cost from twenty-five to thirty thousand dollars, but if you try to sell those vessels to-day and on the auction block they bring approximately only $3,000. There is no demand for them; no one wants them, and the result is that the managing owners cannot advance any more money to operate them, and the banks will not and cannot be expected to advance any more money to operate these
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

vessels this year. If they cease to operate for one year, their markets are gone, or if their debts are not paid the vessels will pass from ownership in the constituency that I represent, and the fleet which has been built up over a period of nearly a century and a half will cease to exist; and the present method of livelihood of approximately half the people who live in the county of Lunenburg will be rendered impossible. Having said that, and it .applies, if not in equal measure, to a greater or less extent, to the fishermen all along the coast of Nova Scotia, whether they operate in boats or vessels, and it is true also of the fishermen of New Brunswick and of the salt fishermen in the Gaspe peninsula, what do we suggest as a remedy?
My hon. friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) did me the honour of quoting from a speech I made in Montreal some time ago, and he invited me to state what we have to suggest as a remedy. At the time that speech was made I was aware that a delegation was waiting on the government at Ottawa, a non-partisan delegation, including among its members my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), asking for certain remedies, and I did not feel that I was at liberty to reveal those remedies until such time as they had been presented to the Prime Minister and his colleagues; but now that they have been presented and are public property I do so without hesitation.
The first remedy asked for was a bonus.
I know that my free trade friends will say that bonusing is unsound. I am not enamoured of the idea of a bonus if I could think of any other method. It is only as a measure of temporary and immediate relief, and if any other method could be suggested I should be glad to consider it, but I have had the opportunity of collaborating with those vitally interested in this industry in my constituency, with men on both sides of politics with whom I have sat in round table conference to discuss the situation and endeavour to find a remedy, and we have not been able to devise any other method. It is purely a temporary expedient, but unless we do get a bonus the paralysis which threatens will grip that fleet and the livelihood of half the people of Lunenburg county will be gone. So I urge the remedy of a bonus for the favourable consideration of the Minister of Finance, and when I ask him for it, I ask the house to remember that we do not ask it for Lunenburg alone, because we quite recognize that what we get must be given to all fishermen similarly situated. But we do ask it because we feel that in no other way can
[Mr. Ernst.)
our industry be saved. It is purely a temporary expedient. To say that the salt fishing industry cannot and will not recuperate is equivalent to losing one's hope and faith in the future so far as the economics of the situation is concerned, and if we are going to face the future in a spirit of hopelessness generally, we might all just as well throw up our hands. But on the contrary, if we look forward to improving conditions, we see no injustice in asking this country for this temporary relief to tide us over this particular time because never in the 150 years of the existence of the industry have we asked anything similar before.
Having suggested a bounty, I come to the second remedy which we propose, and that is trade treaties. We realize that trade treaties cannot offer us any immediate relief, but they can offer us relief for the future. I might be asked, trade treaties with whom. I answer quite frankly, with any country in the world that is willing to take our fish. Again I give you my personal view and the viewpoint of my own constituency; we would say a trade treaty with Cuba. I know the difficulties which present themselves in that connection, the difficulties of the British West Indies treaty, because once you start to negotiate with Cuba immediately you will be told that you cannot negotiate unless you give Cuba a preference on sugar, and you cannot give Cuba a preference on sugar because of the British West Indies treaty. But I say to this house that as far as the maritime provinces are concerned, and I am speaking now not only of the fishing industry but of the potato industry as well, a treaty with Cuba would do more to rejuvenate those provinces than a treaty with any other single country in the world. Porto Rico, of course, does not offer the same opportunities because her tariffs are controlled wholly by the United States. We may be able to do something to help ourselves at the forthcoming Imperial conference, but we must remember that amongst our competitors with whom we shall have to deal are Newfoundland and the British Isles themselves, and what we get, of course, they must get. But even narrowing the field down to that extent would be of material assistance to us. As I said at the outset, trade treaties with almost any salt fish consuming country in the world are desirable to us.
Now I come to the last remedy which I suggest, and that is that we should get, even if it is only within the empire, some stabilization of currency. I am giving purely my own personal view and looking at the problem

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
wholly from my own standpoint and that of my constituency, but from the standpoint of my constituency, which is an exporter, we are by no means eager to bring the Canadian dollar back to par in terms of the American dollar bill. We do, however, want some stability of exchange, because with exchange fluctuating we cannot sell at thirty or ninety days not knowing what we are going to get at the end of that period. This instability makes it almost impossible to do business.
There is nothing further I want to add except this, and again I voice a purely personal view. Coming from Nova Scotia I realize that we cannot for some years to come, in any event, become a highly industrialized community. This is an age of hydroelectric power, and hydro-electric power so far as it is available to us is available only in comparatively small quantities as compared with many of the other provinces of Canada. Until we can get cheap electricity, we cannot become highly industrialized. On the other hand, we do not want to lose sight of the fact that we desire to become industrialized because by no other means can we hope to take care of the natural increase of our population, but until that time comes the industries on which we have to rely are the basic industries-our coal mines, fisheries, farming, and to a lesser extent our timber resources-and anything that can be done to help those industries helps to keep Nova Scotia alive. Personally I look forward to the day, and I do not think it is very far distant, when we shall be able to utilize our coal to produce electric power cheaper than it can be produced from the great rivers of Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, but until that day comes I feel it my duty as one who was born and bred in a constituency in the province of Nova Scotia to press the interests of the greatest basic industry that I have in my constituency, and one which employs in the maritime provinces as many people as the coal and steel industries combined. We only ask the government to give us that fair consideration which they give to other provinces and other industries throughout the dominion.

May I ask one question with regard to the remedy of a bonus which my hon. friend mentioned? What form would that bonus take? Would it be a bonus to each individual fisherman dependent upon the size of the catch?
WTith your permission, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion as to a bonus was a per quintal bonus to each fisherman on his production.

However, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has made certain comments in this debate I feel compelled, on behalf of the province of British Columbia- with which province I now find the province of Quebec should also be associated-to raise once more my voice, even if it be a feeble and. fluttering one, in support of the rights of our province.
I think I might best size up the situation by quoting some remarks I made on June 2,, 1928.
The act-

-what did the act do? It provided that an annual grant-

-not a bounty, a grant, of $160,000 a year be paid. Where was that grant obtained? By looking at section 2 we find that it is to be taken out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.

We have nothing to do with the intention or what somebody thought or did not think- 
When the act was passed.
-we have simply the act to bind us. I have a letter from an official of the department making a very valiant and desperate attempt to justify the action of the government in years past. To make a long story short, Canada sold certain privileges to the United States for $4,500,000.
