There are few members in this house, Mr. Speaker, to whom I listen with greater pleasure than the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. Usually he has the wrong end of the argument, but since he first brought up this matter in 1928 he has been, I might almost say, obstinate in refusing to see this question in its proper light. He appears to have an obsession with regard to this question of the fish bounties, and perhaps for the information of the house it would be well to clear up this matter and find out exactly what the bounty amounts to.
In 1871 the treaty of Washington was agreed upon by Great Britain and United States, and by article 18 of that treaty the fishermen of the United States were given liberty to exercise certain rights in the waters of the coast of the maritime provinces, Quebec and Newfoundland, while equal rights were given our fishermen with regard to United States waters. At that time there was no question of British Columbia or any other place; the question was as to the relative value of the rights which were given. To determine what those rights were worth a commission sat in Halifax.
Have you the names of the commissioners?

I
have not the names here, but most of us remember that one commissioner came from St. John, one from Quebec, one from Prince Edward Island-Sir Louis Davies-and one from Nova Scotia, I think five in all. At all events, as a result of their investigation compensation was fixed at 85,500,000, which was to be paid by the government of the United States to the government of Great Britain. This amount was not paid until January, 1879. Later the British government paid $1,000,000 of the award to Newfoundland and $4,500,000 to the government of Canada.
The amount paid to this country, as the hon. member stated, was put in the consolidated revenue fund, and subsequent to the payment of that amount the claim was advanced by the fishermen of the Atlantic coast that this amount should not be regarded as consolidated revenue but that at least the annual interest on the award should be specifically devoted to the development of the Atlantic coast fisheries. Thus it was determined that the difference in the value of the rights given the fishermen of both countries was $5,500,000. The report to which I am referring goes on to say that it is to be regretted that the legislation empowering the governor in council to authorize the annual grant of $160,000 does not in specific terms state that this amount is for the benefit of the Atlantic coast fisheries. I am referring to the report of the royal commission investigating the fisheries of the maritime provinces.

Of what year?
Mr. MacDONALD (Cape Breton South); The report was issued in 1927. I agree with my hon. friend that this amount never should have been placed in the consolidated revenue fund.

Yes, it should.
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

Are there not certain
conditions imposed before this bounty is paid?
Mr. MacDONALD KCape Breton): The bounty is regulated according to the catch, and so on.
And the time they are engaged in fishing.
And the size of the boat, and so on.

In any case, that procedure has been followed through all the years, and now it is too late for my hon. friend to try to claim a share of that money. I quite agree that the wrong method was taken at that time; the money should have been placed in a trust fund, but the unfortunate thing is that this was not done, and the mistake made at that time has afforded my hon. friend several opportunities to bring forward this claim on behalf of his province.
Hear, hear.

Is it not a fact that the
German reparations payments to this country go into the consolidated fund, just as this money went into it?
Yes, in the same way.
Yes, but the German reparations payments did not disappear for four years, as this money did.

The point I am making is that this money must be regarded by any government as a trust fund to be used for certain purposes. Possibly the time has come when this whole matter should be reconsidered. I am not at all convinced that this payment of bounties is the best way to use this money. I am particularly interested in boat fishermen; I differ with my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst), who is interested in large vessels. My constituents are all poor men along the fringe of the Cape Breton coast; they are all boat fishermen, and they all receive this bounty, which is graded accord-

ing to the size of the boat, the number of men working, the amount of fish caught, and so on. For years this industry has been declining; the fishermen are getting poorer, and in many cases they are leaving their homes. In this report of 1927 the statement is made that the fishing villages along the coast are growing fewer and smaller year by year. That should not be so. Within ten or twelve miles of the coast of Nova Scotia we have the richest fishing area in the world, with enough fish to feed Europe and Canada. We see that industry declining year by year and the fishermen becoming poorer and poorer. It is simply a statement of fact that past governments, Liberal and Conservative, did not have their eyes open to the value of this great natural resource.
Hear, hear.

Even
under present depressed conditions we find eighteen or twenty million dollars a year derived from these fisheries, but unfortunately the industry is declining and the fishing boats are rotting on the shore. Surely with such a great natural resource placed in the hands of our people we should be sufficiently alive to its importance to take the necessary steps to develop it along sound lines.
What is the cure for the present unsatisfactory condition of our fishing industry? Every person who has given the matter the slightest consideration knows that something must be done or the industry will perish. Our fishermen must be given leadership and asistance to equip themselves with boats and nets in order that they may be encouraged to carry on their hazardous calling. Curing plants should be established and transportation facilities provided. This government and the preceding administration have given some attention to providing subsidies for boats and other assistance. But last and possibly most important of all is the necessity of educating cur people to the value of fish as a food. The people of Ontario and the west do not know anything of the food value of fish. Since I have been in Ottawa only on one or two occasions have I had the pleasure of partaking of fish fit to eat. Of course, the people of these parts have no opportunity of judging just how good fish is as a diet. I hope my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins) will not be offended if I tell him that a good, well-cOoked fish is far preferable to the best piece of western beef that ever came off the prairies. The great problem, as I view it, is to instruct the people of Canada as to the food value of good fish. The second

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
problem has to do with putting the fish on their tables. Some work along that line is being done at the present time. Before we talk about securing markets for our fish in other countries, I believe with a proper system of transportation and a proper realization of the food value of fish there is a market in Canada alone for many millions of pounds of this commodity, a market that would be sufficient to place the fishermen of the maritime provinces on their feet and make them prosperous and happy. But to-day it is necessary to begin from the ground up and educate our people to the importance and value of fish in their daily diet.
Now, with regard to the resolution itself, I have no quarrel with it at all. I am in favour of it.
Thank you.

But
T want the resolution broadened out; it should not be confined to the province of Quebec alone. Quebec is in the same category as the maritime provinces. We have this great wealth of fisheries on our Atlantic coast, extending from the St. Lawrence down to Cape Breton and all around Nova Scotia. It is a lamentable fact that in the past those in authority in this country have not realized the value of these fisheries, but it is to be hoped that now the matter has been brought to the attention of the government they will regard it not as a party question at all, but as a national question, and will take such action as will tend properly to develop one of the most important of the natural resources of Canada, -the fisheries of the maritime provinces.

Mr. Speaker, as this discussion has taken more or less of a general trend, and the question of bounties has been brought up, I desire to bring one phase of it to the attention of the house. I regret that neither the acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) nor the former minister of the department (Mr. Rhodes) is in his seat. Possibly members have noticed through the press that there is a strong agitation among the Maine fishermen to place an embargo on the importation of live lobsters into the United States. One of the reasons for the agitation is the very question that we have been discussing this afternoon. They say the fishermen of Canada are subsidized, and that therefore the American fishermen cannot compete with them. I take strong exception to the statement, for I think I am correct in saying that the lobster fishermen of the maritime provinces, especially Prince 41761-83
Edward Island, are not subsidized in any shape or form and do not qualify for the bounty which is paid under the fisheries award. If I am not correct I should like to be put right.

That is right.
Mr. VENIOT. That is right.

I am quite certain that individual lobster fishermen cannot qualify for any bounty, consequently our friends across the border are wrong in the stand they are taking. Recently two bills have been introduced in the Senate of the United States and have received strong support. Their purpose is to impose an embargo on lobsters under ten and a half inches. At the present time our fishermen are allowed to ship into the United States live lobsters measuring nine inches in length. The American fishermen are not allowed to ship in lobsters under ten and a half inches in length. Now they are asking that an embargo be imposed against Canadian lobsters and that the requirement as to size apply to all lobsters offered for sale in the United States, namely 10J inches. I have in my hand a press report in which it is stated:
We are not seeking to keep out Canadian lobsters. Canada can ship all she wants to if she'll follow the proper conservation practices and ship in lobsters of the proper length. Canada subsidized lobster fishermen and their competition had cut prices.
I want to direct the attention of the Department of Fisheries to how seriously such an embargo would affect the lobster fishermen of the maritime provinces. I do hope the minister will take cognizance of what is going on and endeavour to present the facts of the case to the United States Department of Fisheries, because it is absolutely unfair that our fishermen should be treated in this way when our friends across the border are labouring under such a misapprehension of the facts. A few days ago I wrote to the United States authorities. This letter, which was addressed to the Department of Fisheries, Washington, and dated March 16, reads:
Sometime ago newspaper reports stated that the United States government intended putting a duty on live lobsters going into the United States market but recently I have not seen anything in connection with this matter.
Will you kindly let me know if any action has been taken regarding it and at what stage such legislation, if any, is at the present time.
The reply, dated March 18, reads:
Dear Sir:
In reply to your letter of March 16, it is presumed that the newspaper reports mentioned may have referred to bills introduced by Senator White (S. 2370) and Congressman

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

Nelson (H. R. 6586), of Maine which would have prohibited the importation of lobsters less than 101 inches in length which accords with the legal restrictions in the State of Maine. So far as the bureau is aware, neither of these bills have ever been reported out of committee.
Very truly yours,
Lewis Radcliffe,
Acting Commissioner.
It would appear that these bills have not yet come before the house, but are still before the committee. Under date of March 19, I replied as follows:
Your letter received and I wish to thank you for the information contained in same.
By the newspaper reports it would appear that your department is under the impression that our Canadian lobster fishermen are subsidized by the government. This is not quite correct as any fishing bounty given in Canada goes to line fishermen and lobster fishermen alone cannot qualify for the bounty, so that this argument cannot be used.
As I said before, I should like to see the government take up this matter in a departmental way and advise our friends across the border that the lobster fisherman of the maritime provinces is not subsidized, and that this should not be used as an argument for the putting on of an embargo or restriction such as has been suggested. Possibly the former Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes), who is now in his seat, may have some further information on this matter. I know it will be welcomed by the house and by the fishermen of the maritime provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the observations of the last speaker and also with the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald):	I come from the Miramichi district, and unquestionably this river is the greatest salmon fishing river in the *world, as to quality, and second only to the Pacific coast, as to quantity. I should like to speak very briefly in connection with a problem which is of vital importance to the salmon fishermen in this river.
We welcome the American angler to Canadian waters and appreciate the money expended in the payment of guides, the opening up of camps, and the purchase of supplies, but unfortunately at the present time there obtains in certain quarters in New Brunswick the impression that commercial fishing on the Miramichi should be curtailed if not entirely eliminated. Last year I had the pleasure of attending a representative gathering of the various fishing interests held in Chatham, where the Deputy Minister of Fisheries explained the desire of his department that the several interests should cooperate for the
(Mr. MacLean.]
good of this great fishing industry. Unfortunately, conflict exists between the American angler and the set-net men, the anchor men and the drifters, but it is the policy of the department, as enunciated by the deputy minister, to endeavour to arrive at some common ground so that this great asset on the Atlantic can be protected and conserved for the common good.
As I said before, the curtailment of the commercial fishing is being agitated. I think this agitation is being inspired by eminent legal counsel who have seen fit to accept retainers from our American friends to advance the cause of the American angler as opposed to that of the set-net men and drifters. I submit that the interests of the Canadian people are paramount and that there should be no undue interference with the liberties which they have enjoyed from time immemorial. I submit also that the commercial fisherman should cooperate to a reasonable extent with the angler; he should realize the immeasurable benefit which accrues to other sections of the country from the investments of our American friends. I might mention that the Hon. Mr. Justice Maclean, as chairman of the royal commission in 1928, did not make any recommendation as to the curtailment of driftnets. The situation is so serious to our people that in these days of economic distress I submit that any change contemplated should be deferred, at least, until times improve, which we trust will not be in the very distant future.
I am heartily in sympathy with the hon. member who has submitted this resolution to the house for its consideration, but I would have preferred had its principles been extended to the maritime provinces. I realize the absolute need at the present time for economy and that subsidies to our fishermen would of necessity involve a large financial outlay. But the situation is serious, and, consistent with the need for economy in all departments of the public service, I appeal to the administration to consider seriously the representations which have been made and to grant them as far as the finances of the country will permit.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer briefly to the earnest plea which has been made by the fishermen of the Miramichi for a system of cooperative marketing and the provision of adequate cold storage facilities.
May I add that the situation facing the driftnet fishermen of the Miramichi is a vital one. This industry employs a large number of people who have no other possible means

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
of earning a livelihood. We welcome the American to Canada, but I submit, with all due deference to my good friends of the bar who have accepted large retainers, that this is not the time to curtail seriously the liberties of our people. The various interests, including the American angler, should be able to find some common ground upon which to work for the good of the public generally.

The hon. member referred
only to the Miramichi river; does he not mean the bay as well?
I was referring particularly to the river, but my remarks would apply equally to the counties of Gloucester and Kent.

I was afraid the wrong
impression might be given by referring only to the river.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, I am not going to
speak at great length, but I have a few words to say on this matter on behalf of my constituents. First of all, the fish should belong to the people who live along the rivers and streams, to be used for their food, the surplus to be sold on the outside market for the use of people who live at a distance from those rivers and streams. In my constituency, which is fairly large, there are at least 150 lakes and many streams and rivers. I congratulate the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) on his excellent move in directing the attention of the house to the fisheries of this country and more particularly of the province of Quebec. I am sorry to say that the most important lakes and streams of my constituency have been rented to United States citizens through the influence of a legislative councillor, whom I shall not name but whom everyone will recognize, and who by some unknown means has been able to secure leases of those lakes and streams on behalf of foreigners. In fact, last winter at least thirty people, who were not fishing but hunting on the grounds of those landlords, were arrested and had to spend thirty days in gaol.
My idea about fisheries is that, first of all, the people of any particular province should benefit from its own natural resources. I do not know what the conditions are in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia, but in Quebec the fishing industry is a real one. I contend that it should be enjoyed by the citizens of that province, and it is on their behalf that I suggest that the Minister 41761-834
of Fisheries, in case he takes the matter up with the provincial government, see to it that all the leases that have been secured through the influence of that legislative councillor, who was elected a long time ago but who is no longer elected by the people, be cancelled, and that orders be given that in future no recommendation be accepted from him on behalf of any United States or other foreign citizen for the enjoyment of the exclusive privilege of fishing in our territory.

well, but what I say is directly connected with fisheries. I am discussing broadly the question of fisheries, especially as it concerns my constituency. I thank the minister very much, but let me say to him in all earnestness, I shall be delighted if he will be disposed to talk the matter over with the provincial authorities when he meets them. Probably they are not aware of the situation and it should be brought to their attention. I am sure that as soon as the fact is disclosed to

them, they will immediately see to it that the lease's are cancelled, that the people who live along those wonderful streams and lakes have their rights restored to them, so that in future there will be no such reason to complain. This is why I should be glad if the hon. gentleman would say a word in support of the matter. I am sure his wonderful smile shows that he has been convinced.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful indeed to the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain), first of all for having brought up a very interesting question for discussion, and, second, for having informed the house that the absence of the Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) is due to a very sad bereavement in his family. As you know, Mr. Speaker, this morning he was obliged to attend the funeral of a brother to the late Hon. Rodolphe Monty, who was at one time a prominent figure in this house and member of this party.
Before attempting to comment on the resolution submitted to the house by my hon. friend, may I tell him I am rather surprised that he has waited such a long time before asking the federal government to cooperate with the provincial authorities in an endeavour to alleviate the sad situation which confronts the fishermen of Quebec. I am afraid I shall have to crave the indulgence of the house for being obliged to pass in review some of the judgments delivered by the privy council in reference to the question of fisheries.
Before 1922, as it is well known, the federal government was administering the fisheries in Quebec as it does now for the maritime provinces and British Columbia. Under the British North America Act "sea coast and inland fisheries" are, by inclusion in article 12, placed under the jurisdiction of the federal government. No difficulty arose about fisheries between the federal government and the provinces "until about 1882, when the federal government undertook to lease salmon angling privileges in non-tidal rivers in New Brunswick." The privy council held in the famous case of Robertson vs. the Queen that in nontidal waters, the fisheries did not come under the legislative power of the federal government, "but remained the property of the riparian owners."
Following the above decision, the provinces claimed that they had jurisdiction in tidal waters as well, and it was agreed upon between the federal and provincial governments to submit for decision a stated case to the supreme court and finally to the privy council. Lord Haldane, in delivering the judgment of the

lords of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on November 30, 1920, in the case of the Attorney General for the Dominion of Canada against the Attorney General for the province of Quebec, gave a very comprehensive study of the different laws and decisions with respect to the fisheries and the respective rights of the federal government and the governments of the provinces. I shall not venture to quote in full the notes of the learned jurist, but allow me, Mr. Speaker, to draw your attention to the following:
In the province of Quebec, under the old French law and before 1760, "the right of fishing in navigable waters belonged to the domain of the crown and the public enjoyed the right of fishing in such waters, only subject to the prerogative of the king of France, to grant at his pleasure exclusive rights of fishing to individuals." This state of law, however, was altered "by statutes passed after the session of 1763."
It is not necessary for me to dwell at great length on the various statutes passed until the British North America Act became law in 1867.
In the case of the Attorney General for the Dominion vs. the Attorney General for the Provinces, submitted to the privy council in 1898, it has been held that the exclusive power of regulating fisheries, "no matter where they were situated, was vested in the federal government, under the British North America Act, but that any rights which the provinces had prior to confederation were still retained by them." It has been contended that this decision "did not define what were those property rights of the provinces." After the rendering of the said decision in 1898, the provinces along the sea claim the administration of their respective fisheries.
It was decided in 1914, in the case of the Attorney General for British Columbia vs. the attorney general for the dominion (1914-A. C. 153) that:
[DOT]-it was not competent for the legislature of British Columbia to authorize the government of the province to grant exclusive rights of fisheries in tidal rivers or in the sea, including arms of the sea and estuaries of rivers. It was laid down that in the sea wherever the common law of England applies the right of fishing is a public right not dependent on the proprietary-title and that consequently tile regulation of the right must rest exclusively with the Dominion parliament.
It has been said that this decision settled all causes of litigation between the dominion and the provinces, everywhere except in Quebec.
In the province of Quebec, as you know, Mr. Speaker, the law is different from the

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
law of the other provinces. The latter are governed by the common law of England and the former by the civil code and the statutes of the local parliament.
Immediately after the decision of the privy council, in 1914, the Dominion of Canada published, in the official Canada Gazette, a notice stating that on January 1, 1915, "it would assume control of the fisheries in the tidal rivers of the province of Quebec hitherto administered by the federal government" and at the same time, on the 25th of January, the government of the province of Quebec published, in the Quebec Official Gazette, a notice that "the decision of the British Columbia reference did not apply to the province of Quebec and that, therefore, any person wishing to fish in the river and gulf of the St. Lawrence and any tidal waters, should make application to the Department of Colonization, Mines and Fisheries" to obtain the necessary license or permit.
As a result of the fresh controversy which then arose, a new reference to the privy council was agreed upon and in 1914 the case of the Attorney General for the province of Quebec vs. the Attorney General for the Dominion of Canada was submitted to the court of the King's Bench of the province of Quebec, and afterwards to the privy council. That case is precisely the one I referred to a moment, ago, when I quoted the judgment of Lord Haldane. The decision of the privy council was decidedly in favour of the Dominion of Canada. The distinction made by the lords of the privy council is very clear. In tidal waters the power of granting rights of fisheries is vested exclusively in the federal government when the fishing is carried on in the waters without attaching engines or nets to the soil; but when the fishing is carried on by way of fishing nets attached to the soil, the provincial government has the exclusive power to grant the right to affix engines to the soil.
Be that as it may; that decision was not at all a victory for the government of the province of Quebec, as was admitted by the former Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) on April 3, 1922, at page 620 of volume 1 of Hansard for 1922, when he recognized that the decision of the privy council in 1920 gave to the federal government the exclusive power of regulating the fisheries.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that that decision was certainly a very wise one. It marked the end of a long .struggle the sole result of which had been, federally as well as provincially, to divert attention from a basic industry, just as important as agriculture, and to delay
for a quarter of a century the rational organization of our deep sea fisheries. It finally placed Quebec on a basis of equality with the other provinces, permitting it:
(1)	To have a single and complete fishery service: (a) to compel respect for the laws and regulations; (b) to ensure the observance of the treaties concerning foreign fishermen on our coasts;
(2)	To put an end to abusive and indefinite claims derived from certain seigneurial privileges;
(3)	To place the entire service, police and education, under the experienced direction of the federal department, which is equipped with the required means of action;
(4)	To establish a system of cooperation, along well defined lines, 'betwen the federal and provincial governments, in order to revive our deep sea fisheries. The highest authorities of the country, united under the name of Natural Resources Conservation Commission, had already recognized that such cooperation was essential to ensure the full application to the deep sea fisheries of the administration's salutary influence.
(5)	To liberate the provincial treasury from an expensive and difficult service, entailing if it is to be carried to the same degree of perfection and usefulness as those of the maritime provinces, for example, an annual expenditure that cannot be less than $400,000 or $500,000. As these provinces cost the federal treasury over $1,000,000 a year, it is considered that from $400,000 to $500,000 should be allowed to the province of Quebec, where all is yet to be done.
During the season of 1921, in pursuance of the decision of the privy council, the federal Department of Marine and Fisheries assumed the administration of all fisheries "in navigable waters accessible from the sea by navigation." The department drew up and started to carry out the following program of reforms:
(a)	To create a staff of younger men who would follow a course of special studies and secure technical qualifications, etc. To begin with, fish wardens had to be trained, just as agronomists are in agriculture, along the lines already followed in the maritime provinces.
(b)	To increase salaries in order that the new staff should devote its whole time to the fishery service.
(c)	To establish a bureau of fisheries at Quebec.
(d)	To establish an educational centre somewhere in the Gaspe peninsula to meet the immediate requirements of the service, then to develop into a marine biological station, demonstration, study and information centre, etc.
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

(e)	To carry on throughout the province a publicity campaign for the products of the sea, etc., etc.
It is interesting now to ask ourselves whether the government of the province of Quebec at any time in 1921 expressed its willingness to cooperate with the dominion authorities in putting into operation the program of reforms which had been proposed by the federal Department of Fisheries. The government of the province of Quebec was desirous of concealing from the electorate of that province the fact that it had gained nothing in the long and protracted litigation which lasted more than twenty years. It gave the keynote to the Liberal newspapers of the province of Quebec to proclaim that the privy council had recognized the predominant claims of the province over the rights of the federal government. The present hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) on April 3, 1922, admitted in the House of Commons that there was still a conflict as to jurisdicition in the administration of fisheries along the coast. Instead of safeguarding the rights of the fishermen of the province of Quebec the Dominion government in the month of February, 1922, by a mere order in council, transferred the whole administration of Quebec fisheries to the legislature of that province.
May I state, Mr. Speaker, how that came about. Hon. members know that a general election was held in the year 1921. Throughout the campaign in the province of Quebec not a word was uttered on Liberal platforms concerning the administration of fisheries within the province. The Conservative government was defeated at the polls. In the month of January, 1922, the new administration took office. At that time the present hon. member for Quebec East was made Minister of Marine and Fisheries and began to negotiate in camera with the Minister of Fisheries in the province of Quebec. As I have said, in February, 1922, by a mere order in council, without the authority of parliament, the government of the dominion transferred the administration of fisheries to the legislature of the province of Quebec.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Before recess, Mr. Speaker, I was discussing the purport of the order in council passed by the Dominion government on February 14, 1922, transferring the adminis-

tration of fisheries in the province of Quebec to the government of that province. I stated that this order in council, although very far-reaching in its scope, had not been made the subject of public discussion during the federal elections which had taken place only two months before it was passed, and that neither the Liberal candidates for the federal. house nor the premier of Quebec, who took a great part in those elections, let the people of that province know the drastic change which was contemplated with regard to the administration of fisheries.
I would like to know where and in what circumstances the premier of Quebec took such a large part in that federal election.

Mr. Perrault is not
Minister of Fisheries now.

Mr. Perrault is reported to have said that from that time on the province of Quebec would have absolute control over its fisheries, and when a debate took place in the provincial legislature Hon. Mr. Perrault boasted of having achieved such astounding results. The leader of the opposition, who then was Mr. Arthur Sauve, the present Postmaster General, expressed some fears as to the legality of the transfer of such rights which, by the British North America Act, were vested solely in the dominion parliament. He suggested that the provincial government should have some legislation enacted which would really protect the interests of the fishermen of Quebec, but nothing of the sort was done.
The Liberal newspapers, inspired by the leaders of the party at Quebec as well as at Ottawa, took care to proclaim the great victory achieved by the province in preventing the dominion from contributing any money to provide the fishermen of Quebec with an efficient and reasonable service. After having read those remarks I am not surprised that hon. gentlemen opposite have beenjsilent and deaf for eight years and that they never invoked the authority of the federal government to come to the rescue of the fishermen of Quebec. But now, Mr. Speaker, when we have a Conservative administration here in Ottawa, hon. gentlemen opposite proclaim themselves the saviours of the fishermen, and want to have the impression go throughout Quebec that we are not adequately protecting the fishermen of that province, though that province has taken the matter under its own control and this government has been prevented from contributing anything to help those men.
This afternoon, before the dinner hour, I heard the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), helping his friend the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain), ask
that the federal government cooperate with the provincial government. I have before me Hansard for 1922, and I find that the hon. member for Bonaventure brought forward a resolution congratulating the Dominion government, presided over at that time by the present right hon. leader of the opposition, for having secured that great victory for Quebec, in the transfer of the administration of fisheries. I find also the speech made in this house by the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who explained very fully all the different legislation, the orders in council and the judgments of the privy council which had to do with the matter. When Mr. Mc-Quarrie, at that time a distinguished member from British Columbia, rose in his place and put some questions concerning the administration of fisheries in Quebec and in British Columbia, one of the many reasons advanced by the former Minister of Justice to justify the transfer was that the federal government had spent in Quebec $88,000 and had received only $12,000. On April 3, 1922, answering a question put to him by Mr. Ladner, another distinguished member from British Columbia, the former Minister of Justice said:
I do not see how any revenue could be enjoyed in view of the fact that we expended $88,000 last year and the receipts were only $12,000. So the Quebec fisheries will be a charge on the provincial government.
Now, this is the wonderful way in which our friends opposite have seen fit to serve the interests of the fishermen of Quebec. It is no surprise that they who have been deaf and mute for twelve years now say that the exchequer of Quebec has not sufficient revenues, and that this is the reason why the federal government should contribute more towards the Quebec fisheries service.
I am not opposed to the federal government helping the fisheries of Quebec, and I am ready to support the motion; but, Mr. Speaker, I think it is imperative that we on this side of the house should tell the people of Quebec what motives lie behind this motion, and that we should tell of the great betrayal in 1922 of the fishermen of Quebec by our friends opposite. Mr. Meighen, the then leader of the opposition, speaking on the same motion expressed his surprise at the astounding procedure the government had chosen to adopt to get rid of the administration of fisheries, and he added:
The minister's remarks have been of value as interpreting the judgments delivered since 1882 by the privy council. I may go further and say that they are illuminating on every question except those questions which may possibly come in controversy and be of moment in connection with the conduct of administration,
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

that is to say, on the question of the right of the government of Canada to abdicate to any other government a function placed in it by the constitution, the right of the government of Canada by order in council to amend the British North America Act.
The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay and the hon. meiriber for Bonaventure have referred to a delegation which last week interviewed the .provincial Minister of Fisheries at Quebec, .but the former hon. gentleman deemed it wise not to read the memorandum which that delegation then submitted, for it strongly condemned the fisheries administration of the provincial government. The text of this memorandum was published in the Quebec Chronicle-Telegraph on the nineteenth instant. As hon. members know, that newspaper supports the provincial government. This appears on the front page.
The object of our visit, Mr. Minister, is to bring to your kind attention the following facts:
1. Stagnation and decline of our fisheries:
It is an axiom of general knowledge that, "When we do not advance, we recede." In 1922, in the legislative assembly, Mr. Fabien Bugeaud brought to notice our state of stagnation; the total yield of our fisheries has not changed since fifty years. Therefore, if there must be a change, if it is to come soon, it appears that it will come under the heading of a deficit. To back up this assertion, allow me to quote some figures establishing a comparison between the revenues of the Quebec fisheries and those of three other important provinces; New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and British Columbia. These last show a total augmentation of approximately $29,000,000 during this period -while w-e show a decline.
Then they give these figures:
Nova Scotia
1880	$ 6,219,061
1930	 10,411,202
New Brunswick
1880	 2,744,447
1930	 4,853,575
British Columbia
1880	 713,335
1930	 23,103,302
Quebec
1880	 2,631,556
1930	 2,503,998
I ask hon. members to notice that in the fifty years from 1880 to 1930 the fishery revenues of British Columbia increased from $713,335 to the huge sum of $23,103,302, while the fishery revenues of Quebec decreased in that period from $2,631,556 to $2,503,998.
Shame.

Those facts are astounding, and they tend to prove that instead of resorting to litigation for half a century the government of Quebec should have come to an

understanding with the federal government. Now, the only way to remedy the situation is to arrange a conference between the provincial and the federal authorities, to ascertain by what means the interest of the fishermen and the public interest would be best served. Although, as I said a moment ago, this resolution is moved only in order to try to impress on the people of Quebec that the Conservative -party never did anything for the fisheries of Quebec, for my hon. friend knows very well that the federal government has no jurisdiction over the fisheries of Quebec, yet if my humble vote can do something to relieve the sufferings of our fishermen brought about by the misguided policy of our friends opposite when they held office and assumed to transfer the administration of the Quebec fisheries by a mere order in council, a procedure which was ultra vires, and extraordinary-I say if I can do anything to help relieve our fishermen from the disadvantages which they are now labouring under as a result of that ill-advised action, I will vote for the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much attention to the debate and I am in full accord with the purpose of the resolution. I am very much interested indeed in the ultimate settlement of this question, my county being situated in that part of the Gaspe peninsula where the province of Quebec has control of its fisheries, while the Dominion government have control of the Magdalen islands.
I do not quite understand the motives underlying the speech delivered by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon). This is not a question of politics, it is not a question of Conservative or Liberal policy, it is simply a question of helping the fishermen. In 1922 the province of Quebec asked the Dominion government to take over control of the fisheries of the province, because the fishermen, especially those on the Gaspe coast, were in a state of distress. After the war there were no fishing boats on the Gaspe coast, these people not being able to resume fishing operations, and the provincial government asked the Dominion government to cooperate in the control of these fisheries, not simply to have control but to cooperate in the helping of the fishermen of Gaspe and of the province.
I cannot understand the attitude of hon. members opposite, especially those from the province of Quebec. Every time they rise in their places to discuss a matter concerning Quebec, they do not discuss it from the federal angle, but blame everything on

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
Premier Taschereau. It is not the premier's fault that this government is in its present condition. Every time hon. members speak of Quebec they bring in the name of Premier Taschereau. He can handle his own business and I ask this government to handle the business of Canada.
We ask that the government give assistance to the fishermen of Quebec. Only a few years ago the farmers of the west had no need of dominion assistance; the country was prosperous and they were able to take care of their own needs. But a crisis came and the farmers of the west had to ask the federal government for assistance, which was granted last year in the form of a bonus on wheat of five cents per bushel. The same thing is true of Quebec. In past years the fishermen had no need of assistance from the federal government or from the provincial government. During the past ten years the provincial government has helped them to the extent of paying fifty per cent of the cost of the construction of their schooners as well as assistance in the purchasing of equipment. A very grave state of affairs exists to-day on the Gaspe coast and the provincial government alone is not able to grant the assistance required. These people now come to the federal government to ask that they be granted the required relief. The fisheries of the dominion expended in 1929-30, $2,400,000, a large portion of this amount being in the form of taxes paid by the fishermen of Quebec. It is only right that these men now have a share in the expenditures being made by this government. It is up to the federal government to contribute something towards the support of the fishermen of Quebec, and it is because of this that I am in full accord with the resolution moved by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain).

speakeroldname: Mr. L. W. JOHNSTONE (Cape Breton North-Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this discussion closes I should like to make a few remarks. The ground has been covered very ably by the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Ernst) and there is very little more to be said. However, as I represent a constituency in which there are a great number of fishermen, I feel that I should say a few words on their behalf.
I am in accord with the resolution moved this afternoon by the hon. member (Mr. Casgrain) but I would have liked to have seen it phrased in broader terms. He should have made his resolution apply to coastal water generally. The situation facing the fishing industry is serious. In Cape Breton
we are confronted with the interference of outside fishermen and the high price of bait.
Only to-day I received a letter from a fisherman in my constituency complaining about the Newfoundland fishermen coming into Antigonish and other ports on the northern coast. These men catch and clean their fish outside and then come into our ports to salt their catch, and they interfere with the rights of our own fishermen.
Another very serious question is that of bait. These men want cold storage facilities provided in Cape Breton. There is one plant there already, one-third of which is owned by the government, but it has been leased to a private concern and our fishermen cannot obtain their bait at reasonable prices, and this is causing great distress at the present time. The price of bait asked by the local firms is so high that the men cannot afford to buy it, and there are no cold storage facilities provided for the storage of their own bait. It would be of great assistance to the fishermen if they could obtain their bait at a proper price.
The lack of markets is a great problem, and I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) that Canada should provide a market for our fish. I do not desire to say anything detrimental to the cooking abilities of Canadian women, but I contend that they should be educated in the use of our fish. An attempt has been made to educate Canadians to use coke instead of foreign coal, and similar education could be carried on in connection with our fish. The women of Canada should be taught how to use and cook Canadian fish.
I am sure that this resolution will do some good because it has provided the opportunity for a discussion of this question. I feel quite confident that the government will take such action as will improve the condition of a very important part of our population.

Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from a county where over half of the population earns its livelihood by fishing, I think I should be lax in my duty if I allowed this opportunity to pass without saying a word or two, even though the resolution pertains only to the province of Quebec. I regret that the hon. member who introduced the resolution (Mr. Casgrain) did not make it dominion-wide. He bases his resolution on the fact that the province of Quebec, which administers its own fisheries, is not now in a position to give the required assistance to the fishermen of that province, and he asks for cooperation between the governments of the
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

province of Quebec and the Dominion of Canada.
I regret that this resolution has been taken as an excuse for political discussion, but since it has drifted into the realm of politics, may I point out to hon. gentlemen opposite from the province of Quebec that Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island do not administer the fisheries of their respective provinces. If the fact that the government of Quebec has jurisdiction over its own fishermen has brought about chaos, as my hon. friend attempts to show, what must we say of the last two or three years of the administration by the federal government of the fisheries in the three maritime provinces?
I am not going to lay upon any government the blame for the depression in the fishing industry. During the last two years especially, the fishermen of Nova Scotia have been repeatedly asking the federal government, and rightly so, to come to their assistance. Even when times were good, even from 1926 to 1929, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as well as Prince Edward Island fishermen appealed to the federal government for greater encouragement. Why? Because, owing to the greater development of the fishing industry in European countries, we could not get the markets that we previously had. For that reason the governments of the three maritime provinces took upon themselves the responsibility of appealing to the federal government, even under the Duncan report, to do something for the fishermen. Therefore I take it that the condition existing in Quebec to-day is not because of the fact that jurisdiction over the fisheries in that province was transferred to the provincial government in 1922.
Having said that much about the political aspect of the matter, may I be permitted to draw the attention of the house to the fishing industry in the maritime provinces, and especially in New Brunswick. I am not doing this in order to criticize the government of the day. I firmly believe you cannot attribute present conditions in the fishing industry in New Brunswick to the government of the day or to any other. As I have explained before, circumstances have arisen which have placed our fishermen in a position which renders it very difficult for them to make a livelihood as they did in former years. But there is one thing which governments can do in the matter of regulation for the conservation of the fishing industry. In mentioning that point, may I call the attention of the government to the regulation governing lobster fishing? For years and years there has existed in New Brunswick a regulation which divides the

province into different fishing seasons of lobsters. For instance, there is an imaginary line drawn from Ste. Anne in the county of Kent to Cape Tormentine. Under the regulation establishing those limits lobster can be fished in that section in the fall of the year. Many fishermen further north in Ste. Anne du Bocage claim that line should be extended to include the whole north shore and that the spring season should be abolished.
What are the conditions? In the counties of Kent and Westmorland, lobster fishermen can fish in the fall of the year, I think from August 15 to October 15. What happens? The fishermen in Kent and Westmorland west of the dividing line, during the spring season of fishing north of that line, go up into Northumberland, Gloucester and Restigouche and fish during that season. Then when the spring season is over, they go back to their homes and fish during the fall up to the 15th of October. In this way they have two fishing seasons whereas our fishermen north of the line, as far north as Restigouche county, have only the one. There is at present a petition before the Department of Fisheries requesting a change in the fishing season in the nothem section of the province, and I hope the department will consider it very carefully. I am told that owing to scientific reasons the date should not be changed; that if we change the date, we may contribute to the rapid destruction of lobsters in northern New Brunswick. Storms in northern New Brunswick during the winter have caused more destruction to the lobster industry that lack of proper regulations. During the storm in the latter part of December of last year, it was estimated that 100 tons or more of live lobsters were driven ashore in the gulf of St. Lawrence on the island of Miscou, Shippigan island, the mainland of Shippigan down as far as Tracadie beach. These lobsters died on the beach. I am not saying that the government should establish a regulation to prevent such an occurrence, but I wish to point out that nature at times causes more destruction to the lobster industry than any lack of regulation.
We know there is poaching, and if there is poaching in any line of the fishing industry it is in regard to lobsters. Education is required to teach those people that they should give up poaching. There is no doubt they will give it up in the very late season, but between seasons, from the middle of June to the middle of August, is the period when the regulations should be strictly enforced, because it is the time in that section when the lobster sheds its shell and, and so to speak, takes on a new dress. But between

Mantime Fisheries, Quebec
August 15 and October 15, the lobster shell is just as hard and firm in the waters of northern New Brunswick as it is in the section of the province where the fishermen are permitted to fish during that period. I would ask the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), who was formerly Minister of Fisheries to extend to the present Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) his knowledge of the situation and not to give too much heed to the theorists, who, calling themselves scientific men, are preventing the fishermen of northern New Brunswick from earning an honest livelihood.
Another question touched upon by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) was that of salted fish. I am in full accord with him on this subject. It is absolutely necessary in these trying times of depression that we should give more encouragement to our fishermen. I do not believe in a bonus, but as the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg said this afternoon, if that is the only means which this government can devise to help out our fishermen, I should be willing to support it. We have been asked to give our support to a bonus to help the farmers of the west, and I willingly and cheerfully agreed to that because it was pointed out to us that that was the only way in which those farmers could be helped at that time. We have also given a bonus to the coal industry in Nova Scotia, and with that I also agreed. Now we are asking that some encouragement be given to an industry which to my mind is greater even than the mining industry in the maritime provinces.. Our fishemen by the thousands and hundreds of thousands are suffering to-day because they cannot get a proper market or a proper price for their fish, and if there is no other way to help them except by a bonus, if they cannot obtain the markets which formerly gave them a reasonable living price for their products, then I would agree to a bonus of so much to each fisherman; or perhaps one way to help would be to assist in the construction and maintenance of the vessels that are used in carrying on that business and which cost so much.
I am not going to discuss to-night the salmon branch of the fishing industry, because I dealt with that last winter, and the one reproach that I have to make to the Minister of Fisheries of that day-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only one?

Only one. My one reproach is this: He promised that he would come and visit our salmon nets last summer and see how our fishermen laboured to catch the salmon, and he did not keep that promise. I know
he was a busy man, but he was not too busy, Mr. Speaker, to spend a day or two on the Restigouche. He was not too busy to enjoy the hospitality of those American gentlemen who to-day are claiming that they should have rights over the fishermen of the province of New Brunswick. I am going to say to the present Minister of Finance that that invitation for him to come and visit our salmon fisheries is still open. He may reply: I am not the Minister of Fisheries; there is an Acting Minister of Fisheries; invite him. No, Mr. Speaker, because the present Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau), when a delegation appeared before him two weeks ago, although he received us in a kindly way and was very courteous, admitted quite openly- I compliment him upon his frankness-that he knew absolutely nothing about salmon or fishing, not even about the casting of a line. Therefore I want somebody to come on tfie spot who knows something about angling.
You know all about firing postmasters.

I have fired postmasters, but I have never fired one-tenth of the number that have been fired since your party came into power; and I am not blaming the Postmastet General for doing the firing but those hungry Tories ait his back. I am a little surprised, Mr. Speaker, that on a question of this importance the hon. member who interrupted has nothing more to say than that. I am sure his constituents would be pleased if they saw that he had once stood on the floor of this house and delivered a sensible speech that would be reported in Hansard, instead of interrupting hon. members who are trying to do their duty in this house.
I am not going to take up the time of the house further, except once more to draw the attention of the Department of Fisheries to the petition that is now before them touching the change of date in the lobster fishing in the northern section of New Brunswick.

I shall try to be brief in my remarks, Mr. Speaker. The discussion on the resolution has been going on for some time; I never thought it would be so lengthy. The consensus of opinion among the members of the house seems to be in favour of the adoption of this resolution and I am pleased that both members from the maritime provinces and members from the province of Quebec on the government side are willing to support my motion.
There is one thing I should like to point out, however. Although the hon. member for
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) has discussed this question in the way he has, and launched upon an attack against what he 'Called the bad administration of the fisheries in the province of Quebec due to the fisheries having come under the control of the provincial government in recent years, he seems to be not quite in accord with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), who this afternoon stated that nothing had been taken away from the fishermen of the province of Quebec, because they had still the right to avail themselves of the various provisions that are on our statute books, such as the federal grant of seventy-five per cent for refrigerators for bait, and the regular grant of thirty per cent for other refrigerators which are necessary for fishermen. The difficulty is-and it is the reason for this motion-that the fishermen in the province of Quebec, and more especially on the north shore of the river St. Lawrence, are in a very unfortunate situation at the present time, having had a poor catch of fish for the last few years; therefore they are not in a position to avail themselves of any such grants or to contribute in the proportion which the law requires before they can obtain these refrigeration facilities. The consequence is that last year and the year before the provincial government has had to do practically everything on its own account in the way of establishing these refrigerator plants on the north shore of the river St. Lawrence in my county. As far as other laws on the statute book of which fishermen might take advantage are concerned, they are not in a position to do so, and since the administration of the fisheries was entrusted to the provincial government in 1922, it has had to do everything on its own account. The revenues derived from the fisheries by the provincial government, I am informed, although I have not exact figures, amount to hardly one per cent of the amount which the provincial government is spending nearly every year on the fisheries of the province, which is $300,000. When the provincial government was entrusted with the administration of the fisheries in 1922, it was due to the fact that it was desired to avoid the difficulties that had prevailed before with respect to licences in interior waters and also in deep and salt water down the lower part of the gulf. That is one of the reasons why the provincial government took over the administration of the fisheries as they stood within the limits of the province of Quebec. Now if the administration of the fisheries by the government of the province of Quebec has been bad, although my hon. friend from Dorchester claims that the

blame should be laid at the door of the provincial government, surely the same blame should be laid at the door of this federal administration when we find conditions obtaining in the maritime provinces as they have been represented by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot). 'Conditions there do not seem to be much better than in the province of Quebec. If the federal administration did not do well in turning over to the provincial government the administration of the law, not the rights of the fishermen, as was suggested by the hon. member for Dorchester, I say, Mr. Speaker, that this government is here to settle all ills. They were elected to give better and more efficient administration, to settle all existing difficulties, to bring back prosperity, happiness and plenty to all. As I have said, I am merely asking that they give the necessary help to the province of Quebec, and I have given my reasons.
I wish to touch upon another point-and for this reason I hope hon. members will hear me a few moments more. The hon. member for Dorchester says we have been absolutely silent for the past eight years, that nothing has been done since the administration of the fisheries was turned over to the government of the province of Quebec. I was not a member sitting for the county of Saguenay on the north shore of the river St. Lawrence when the administration of the fisheries was transferred to the provincial government of Quebec. I was then sitting for the county of Charlevoix-Montmorency. In that district there were not very many fishermen, and the conditions affecting the deep sea fisheries did not obtain there as they do now on the north shore of 'the St. Lawrence. Since the year 1926 I have represented in this House of Commons the county of Saguenay on the north shore of the river St. Lawrence, and have been deeply interested in the fisheries. I have been working much more than my hon. friend from Dorchester would lead the house to believe. If he were to refer to the royal commission which investigated the fisheries of the maritime provinces and the Magdalen Islands he would find that on March 20 in the year 1928 the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay appeared before the commission and presented a brief in the interests of the fishermen along the north shore of the St. Lawrence. At pages 85 and 86 of the report of that commission, issued in the year 1928, my hon. friend will see that the commissioners took cognizance of certain remarks that I made at that time in the interests of the fishermen in my constituency. I shall not take the time to read all the comments contained in this report,

Maritime Fisheries, Quebec
because theTe are many paragraphs which might not be of interest to all hon. members. There are certain points however to which I think I should direct the attention of the house. At page 86 of the report I find the following:
In marketing the fish products of the Gaspe peninsula and the north shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence, most of which is without railway-communication, and is completely isolated during many months of the year, shippers have to rely upon subsidized steamship services performed under contract by the Clarke Steamship Company.
Then, further on in the report I find the following:
Accordingly, there is a demand for improvement in the service performed by the Clarke Steamship Company. We recommend a consideration of the existing contract with the view of affording to this section of the country more adequate transportation facilities.
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter entirely within the jurisdiction of this parliament and the Department of Trade and Commerce. Following the report to w'hich I have referred endeavours were made successfully to secure an enlargement of the subsidies so that adequate facilities, such as refrigeration services in the boats of the Clarke Steamship Company, might be had on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. I am told that such service was extended to the boats of the same company plying between Quebec and the Gaspe peninsula.
I find in the report the further paragraph:
Railway freight and express rates are also complained of in that portion of the Gaspe peninsula which has railway connection.
Railway facilities are under the control of this parliament, and are matters of which this government should take cognizance. In the report a further request was made for harbour improvements or shelters for shore boats on the Gaspe peninsula. At the same time I appeared before the commission, I mentioned that such facilities should be afforded to people along the north shore of the river St. Lawrence.
If hon. members in this house or people outside the house would look at some of the estimates tabled in the years 1928, 1929 and 1930, they would surely find out that your humble servant has not been remiss in the discharge of his duties, because on many occasions I was rebuked by hon. members who then constituted the opposition, and was taken to task even by some members in my own party, because I was asking for too many improvements, such as wharf accommodation, dredging, and harbours, to benefit the fishermen on the north shore. The government implemented part of this report of the commission by paying attention to some of the requests made and by improving facilities at many points along the north shore. That is true more especially at a place called Tunday river, where a wharf was needed, and at Bredor Bay, near Labrador, where similar work was necessary. Many little harbours and breakwaters have been built to help the fishermen, and to implement the report made by this commission.
There is another paragraph in the report dealing with matters which might well be developed by the Department of Fisheries in the province of Quebec. I refer to the grading and inspection of fish, the establishment of a technological and biological laboratory for experiments, the institution of a bureau of information, a scientific study of the oceanography of the river and gulf of St. Lawrence, the migration of the different species of fish, the making of fishing charts, the adoption of a policy of subsidies for cold storage plants, fish canning factories, drying establishments and reduction plants. I think the provincial government in Quebec, which now looks after the administration of law's concerning the fisheries, has begun to deal with the matters here mentioned in the report. As I stated previously the amount required from year to year is far greater than the province of Quebec can afford to spend. The need is always increasing, and there is the added reason that in the years 1930 and 1931, the catch has been small along the north shore of the St. Lawrence. A large amount of the money which might have been divided to help the services mentioned in this report was given by way of subsidy or relief to the people along the north shore of the river. That was the condition obtaining before the relief measures were passed two years ago in this House of Commons.
So, Mr. Speaker, although hon. members opposite may want the country to believe that the hon. member representing Charlevoix-Saguenay has not discharged his duty, it is quite clear they are not stating the facts. Since I have represented that constituency I have given my best attention to the needs of the fishermen. If in the years 1929 and 1930, the government was not approached to secure the relief now described in the resolution, it was because conditions at that time were not so bad. Our markets had not been closed, and the fishermen were in a position to dispose of their product at reasonable prices. To-day they are in a much different position, and it is for that reason this resolution has been introduced before the house.
Maritime Fisheries, Quebec

This afternoon I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg say he was going to take this matter up with the government with a view to helping the fishermen. Apparently three remedies were suggested. The first was a bonus to be given to the fishermen; the second, trade treaties, and the third, the stabilization of currency. If some of those remedies could be applied, fishermen not only in the province of Quebec but also along Atlantic and Pacific sea coasts would receive some benefit.
If we are soliciting federal assistance, it is so that there may be established on the coast of Gaspe, and possibly on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, biological and experimental stations from which the fishermen would be able to obtain information required, such as meteorological reports. Such reports should be printed in the French language. May I call the attention of the house to the fact that two-thirds of the fishermen in the province of Quebec are French, and they cannot take full advantage of all the valuable work that has been done at the biological stations if the results of that work are not translated into French. These stations are far away, and the fishermen cannot go to St. Andrews and Halifax from their own towns or villages on the north shore of the St. Lawrence in order to obtain information. I have in my hand a letter which I addressed last year to the Department of Fisheries, asking for a number of publications which I thought might be of interest to the fishermen in my district. I found that the French edition of a pamphlet entitled "Dried Cod Fisheries" was almost exhausted. Who is to blame for that?
These things should not be allowed to go on if we really want to help the fishermen in Quebec. Measures should be taken also to develop our fish trade more than it has been developed in the past. This might be done by .[DOT]educing the cost of transportation and creating local markets for our fresh fish. If this were done it would be of great help to the fishermen in my constituency.
I did not introduce this resolution because I wanted to play politics at all, as the hon. member for Dorchester suggested; I did not bring up this matter at the request of any person in the provincial government. As I said in my opening remarks, a similar resolution was adopted by the provincial house, after being introduced by the local member for my county, and I thought it behooved me to lay the case before this house with regard to the fisheries of Quebec. I think a bonne entente might be arrived at, and by coopera-
tion and conference between the two governments the little troubles that have existed in the past may be ironed ,out and we might start anew in order to help the fishing industry in Quebec as it should be helped.
